Canonical: https://oathwallet.org/networks/bitcoin

# Bitcoin wallet: send and receive BTC

Receive native BTC with your Oath address and review your Bitcoin network fee before sending.

## Receive Bitcoin

1. Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Bitcoin in Receive.
2. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender.
3. Choose a Bitcoin address format the sending service supports. Oath supports compatible Taproot, SegWit and Legacy accounts; the available choices depend on your wallet.
4. After the sender broadcasts the transfer, follow its status in Oath. Network confirmation can take time.

## Send BTC

1. Open Send and select the asset on Bitcoin. Paste the recipient’s address or scan their QR.
2. Bitcoin fees depend on transaction size and selected inputs. Max accounts for the fee. This is on-chain Bitcoin, not a Lightning invoice.
3. Enter the amount and any required memo or tag. Compare the complete destination with the recipient’s instructions.
4. Review the asset, network, amount and fee, then confirm in Oath. Follow the transaction status after broadcast.

## dApp connections

Connect to compatible Bitcoin dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app.

1. Open a trusted dApp and choose Oath if it is listed, or choose WalletConnect.
2. On desktop, scan the connection QR with Oath. On iPhone or iPad, use a compatible app link or the connection option offered by the dApp.
3. Review the website, selected wallet, Bitcoin network and requested permissions before approving.
4. Review each signing request separately. Disconnect the session from Oath when you are finished.

## Questions

### How do I receive Bitcoin in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Bitcoin in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. Choose a Bitcoin address format the sending service supports. Oath supports compatible Taproot, SegWit and Legacy accounts; the available choices depend on your wallet.

### What pays the Bitcoin transaction fee?

BTC is the native fee asset for this network account. Bitcoin fees depend on transaction size and selected inputs. Max accounts for the fee. This is on-chain Bitcoin, not a Lightning invoice.

### Can I connect Bitcoin dApps?

Connect to compatible Bitcoin dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

Features depend on the app version, network, wallet type and the service you connect to. Check the available actions in your installed app before transferring.

# Solana wallet: send and receive SOL

4. After the sender broadcasts the transfer, follow its status in Oath. Network confirmation can take time.

## Send SOL

1. Open Send and select the asset on Solana. Paste the recipient’s address or scan their QR.
2. Keep SOL for fees and any required token-account creation. Review the fee and remaining balance before confirming.
3. Enter the amount and any required memo or tag. Compare the complete destination with the recipient’s instructions.
4. Review the asset, network, amount and fee, then confirm in Oath. Follow the transaction status after broadcast.

## dApp connections

Connect to compatible Solana dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app. A website that only detects browser extensions may not offer a compatible mobile connection.

1. Open a trusted dApp and choose Oath if it is listed, or choose WalletConnect.
2. On desktop, scan the connection QR with Oath. On iPhone or iPad, use a compatible app link or the connection option offered by the dApp.
3. Review the website, selected wallet, Solana network and requested permissions before approving.
4. Review each signing request separately. Disconnect the session from Oath when you are finished.

## Questions

### How do I receive Solana in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Solana in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. Use the Solana address in Receive. Match a token by its mint and network, not its symbol alone.

### What pays the Solana transaction fee?

SOL is the native fee asset for this network account. Keep SOL for fees and any required token-account creation. Review the fee and remaining balance before confirming.

### Can I connect Solana dApps?

Connect to compatible Solana dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app. A website that only detects browser extensions may not offer a compatible mobile connection.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

Features depend on the app version, network, wallet type and the service you connect to. Check the available actions in your installed app before transferring.

# Gram wallet: send and receive GRAM

Send and receive Gram on iPhone and iPad with Oath Wallet. Gram (GRAM) is the native coin of the TON blockchain, formerly called Toncoin.

## Receive Gram

1. Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Gram in Receive.
2. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender.
3. Choose Gram in Receive and share the TON address shown in Oath. Confirm the sender supports the address format and add a comment if the receiving service requires one.
4. After the sender broadcasts the transfer, follow its status in Oath. Network confirmation can take time.

## Send GRAM

1. Open Send and select the asset on Gram. Paste the recipient’s address or scan their QR.
2. Keep Gram for network fees and any wallet-contract activation. For a jetton, check its master contract; a token named GRAM is not necessarily the native coin.
3. Enter the amount and any required memo or tag. Compare the complete destination with the recipient’s instructions.
4. Review the asset, network, amount and fee, then confirm in Oath. Follow the transaction status after broadcast.

## dApp connections

Connect to compatible Gram dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app. WalletConnect and TON Connect are different protocols. This guide does not claim TON Connect support.

1. Open a trusted dApp and choose Oath if it is listed, or choose WalletConnect.
2. On desktop, scan the connection QR with Oath. On iPhone or iPad, use a compatible app link or the connection option offered by the dApp.
3. Review the website, selected wallet, Gram network and requested permissions before approving.
4. Review each signing request separately. Disconnect the session from Oath when you are finished.

## Questions

### Is Gram the same as TON?

Gram (GRAM) is the native coin formerly called Toncoin. The blockchain remains The Open Network (TON). Confirm you are selecting the native coin, not a similarly named jetton.

### How do I receive Gram in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Gram in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. Choose Gram in Receive and share the TON address shown in Oath. Confirm the sender supports the address format and add a comment if the receiving service requires one.

### What pays the Gram transaction fee?

GRAM is the native fee asset for this network account. Keep Gram for network fees and any wallet-contract activation. For a jetton, check its master contract; a token named GRAM is not necessarily the native coin.

### Can I connect Gram dApps?

Connect to compatible Gram dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app. WalletConnect and TON Connect are different protocols. This guide does not claim TON Connect support.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

Features depend on the app version, network, wallet type and the service you connect to. Check the available actions in your installed app before transferring.

1. Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Bitcoin Cash in Receive.
2. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender.
3. Use the Bitcoin Cash address shown in Receive. Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin are separate networks; do not send BTC to a BCH deposit.
4. After the sender broadcasts the transfer, follow its status in Oath. Network confirmation can take time.

## Send BCH

1. Open Send and select the asset on Bitcoin Cash. Paste the recipient’s address or scan their QR.
2. Review the BCH amount, destination and network fee. A familiar address format does not make a Bitcoin transfer compatible.
3. Enter the amount and any required memo or tag. Compare the complete destination with the recipient’s instructions.
4. Review the asset, network, amount and fee, then confirm in Oath. Follow the transaction status after broadcast.

## dApp connections

Bitcoin Cash send and receive support does not include a supported dApp connection route in this guide. Use Oath for transfers; do not import your recovery phrase into a website to connect.



## Questions

### How do I receive Bitcoin Cash in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Bitcoin Cash in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. Use the Bitcoin Cash address shown in Receive. Bitcoin Cash and Bitcoin are separate networks; do not send BTC to a BCH deposit.

### What pays the Bitcoin Cash transaction fee?

BCH is the native fee asset for this network account. Review the BCH amount, destination and network fee. A familiar address format does not make a Bitcoin transfer compatible.

### Can I connect Bitcoin Cash dApps?

Bitcoin Cash send and receive support does not include a supported dApp connection route in this guide. Use Oath for transfers; do not import your recovery phrase into a website to connect.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

Features depend on the app version, network, wallet type and the service you connect to. Check the available actions in your installed app before transferring.

Connect to compatible Filecoin dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app.

1. Open a trusted dApp and choose Oath if it is listed, or choose WalletConnect.
2. On desktop, scan the connection QR with Oath. On iPhone or iPad, use a compatible app link or the connection option offered by the dApp.
3. Review the website, selected wallet, Filecoin network and requested permissions before approving.
4. Review each signing request separately. Disconnect the session from Oath when you are finished.

## Questions

### How do I receive Filecoin in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Filecoin in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. This account uses Filecoin EVM. Confirm that the destination accepts the address format shown by Oath; do not assume every Filecoin address type is interchangeable.

### What pays the Filecoin transaction fee?

FIL is the native fee asset for this network account. Keep FIL available for network fees. For tokens, check the contract and amount, then review the destination and estimated fee in Oath.

### Can I connect Filecoin dApps?

Connect to compatible Filecoin dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

Features depend on the app version, network, wallet type and the service you connect to. Check the available actions in your installed app before transferring.

1. Open a trusted dApp and choose Oath if it is listed, or choose WalletConnect.
2. On desktop, scan the connection QR with Oath. On iPhone or iPad, use a compatible app link or the connection option offered by the dApp.
3. Review the website, selected wallet, Telos network and requested permissions before approving.
4. Review each signing request separately. Disconnect the session from Oath when you are finished.

## Questions

### How do I receive Telos in Oath?

Open Oath, select your wallet and choose Telos in Receive. Copy the receiving address or show its QR code. Confirm the exact network with the sender. This account is Telos EVM, not Telos Zero or an Antelope account.

### What pays the Telos transaction fee?

TLOS is the native fee asset for this network account. Keep TLOS available for network fees. For tokens, check the contract and amount, then review the destination and estimated fee in Oath.

### Can I connect Telos dApps?

Connect to compatible Telos dApps through WalletConnect. The website must request a network and signing method supported by Oath. Review every connection and signing request in the app.

### Can I send to the same address on another network?

Only send using the network the recipient explicitly supports. A matching address or ticker does not bridge assets or make different chains interchangeable.

# Oath — A wallet, not a marketplace.

Oath is a self-custody Bitcoin and crypto wallet for iPhone and iPad. You control your wallet credentials, review fees before confirming, and manage supported assets without a trading marketplace.

- [Download Oath on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oath-bitcoin-crypto-wallet/id6780187283) — free, for iPhone and iPad
- [Features](https://oathwallet.org/features) · [Support](https://oathwallet.org/support) · [Press kit](https://oathwallet.org/press)

## Why Oath

Most crypto apps want you to trade. Oath wants you to own. No tickers shouting, no casino lights, no one holding your coins for you. Just your money, kept.

## What Oath supports

- Keep wallet credentials on your device and sign transactions locally.
- Create a recovery phrase, or use physical entropy with care.
- Restore supported wallet formats; keep any extra BIP-39 passphrase.
- Use optional password-encrypted iCloud backup with its matching backup file.
- Choose supported Bitcoin address types and inspect EVM approvals.
- Review network fees before confirming a transaction.
- Read the [public source and security scope](https://oathwallet.org/security).

Capabilities depend on the network and release. Silent Payments receiving and discovery are not supported in 4.1.14.

## Self-custody, explained

### What is a self-custody crypto wallet?

A self-custody, or non-custodial, wallet lets you authorize transactions with your wallet’s private keys. The crypto remains recorded on its blockchain. Your wallet helps you manage the credentials and addresses used to access it. Keeping a usable recovery method is your responsibility.

[Understand Oath’s security model](https://oathwallet.org/security)

### How is a wallet different from an exchange account?

With a custodial exchange account, the provider controls the withdrawal keys. With self-custody, you manage the signing credentials. This removes reliance on an exchange to approve a withdrawal, but it also means a forgotten recovery phrase, a malicious approval or a mistaken transfer can cause permanent loss.

[Explore Oath Wallet features](https://oathwallet.org/features)

### Can I use Oath for Bitcoin and other crypto on iPhone?

Oath Wallet is available for iPhone and iPad. Choose the asset and network in the app before sharing a receiving address. A matching coin name or address format does not mean two networks are interchangeable. Available actions depend on your app version, network and wallet type.

[Check supported networks](https://oathwallet.org/networks)

### What happens if I lose my phone?

Recovery depends on the backup you prepared before the loss. A recovery phrase may also require its separate BIP-39 passphrase. Oath’s optional iCloud recovery needs the encrypted backup and the backup password. Check your recovery method before relying on it, and never share recovery words with support.

[Read the backup checklist](https://help.oathwallet.org/collections/backup)

### Is Oath free, and why do transfers have fees?

Oath is free to download from the App Store. Blockchain transfers can require network fees, account reserves or activation costs. These vary by network and conditions. Review the asset, destination, network and fee before confirming; an on-chain transfer generally cannot be reversed.

[Learn about network fees](https://articles.oathwallet.org/where-crypto-network-fees-actually-go)

### Does open source mean a wallet has been audited?

Public code lets people inspect an implementation. It does not by itself establish an independent security audit or prove that the app installed on a phone matches that code. Oath publishes its source-review scope and limitations so you can check the evidence behind a claim.

[Read about source and verifiable builds](https://articles.oathwallet.org/open-source-wallets-verifiable-builds)

# Oath features

Everything you need. Nothing you don’t.

## 01. Create or import a recovery phrase

New wallets use BIP39. Import supported BIP39, Electrum and aezeed phrases in their original format. Electrum and aezeed recover supported Bitcoin accounts and require manual recovery backups; they are not eligible for iCloud backup in 4.1.14.

## 02. Restore an encrypted backup

Restore an existing encrypted Oath backup using its backup password and the backup file in iCloud Drive. Keep a separate recovery-phrase backup and any extra BIP-39 passphrase.

## 03. 57 app localizations

Oath is available in 57 app localizations, with right-to-left layouts, local number formats and BIP39 word lists.

## 04. Open source, with a documented review scope

The full source code is public on GitHub at https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet. The published release includes its security model, verification record and reporting policy. Public source is available for review; it does not establish an independent audit or a verified match to the App Store binary.

## 05. Bitcoin address options

Compatible Bitcoin wallets support Taproot, Native SegWit, nested SegWit and Legacy, depending on the imported material. Capabilities vary by network. Oath 4.1.14 does not support Silent Payments receiving or discovery; see the Silent Payments guide before relying on that feature.

## 06. EVM Access

A tool that shows discovered token approvals (web3 permissions) on supported EVM networks and lets the user submit supported revocation transactions. Revoking is an on-chain transaction with a network fee shown before confirming.

## 07. Your display currency

Choose from the app’s supported display currencies. Values are estimates based on available exchange-rate data.

## 08. Available market prices

See available price quotes for supported assets. Quotes can be delayed or unavailable; displayed fiat values are estimates.

[Download Oath on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/oath-bitcoin-crypto-wallet/id6780187283)

# Oath Wallet security

Oath Wallet keeps recovery input and signing credentials in its protected local vault. Optional encrypted iCloud backups, deliberate exports and WalletConnect requests have separate user-controlled boundaries.

## Open source and App Store builds

The technical descriptions and source excerpts on this page were checked on 30 October 2026 against Oath Wallet **4.1.14 (98)**, source tag **v4.1.14**. Version 4.1.14 (98) is a public source release. No App Store Connect upload or review submission was started for this source release. See its release record for the completed checks; source publication does not establish a match to an App Store download.

Read the [4.1.14 release verification record](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/releases/tag/v4.1.14), [current security model](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/main/Documentation/SecurityModel.md), and [security reporting policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/policy). Provider configuration and Apple signing are supplied through encrypted GitHub deployment secrets and excluded from public source.

## What the checks establish

The release record covers source inspection, secret scanning, compilation and focused host tests. No simulator or physical-device checks were run for build 98. It does not establish an independent security audit or an independently reproduced comparison with an App Store download. Apple approval alone would not establish either result.

## Recovery formats and local signing

New standard wallets use a 12-word BIP39 recovery phrase. BIP39 imports validate supported word lists and checksums locally. Electrum and aezeed imports use their own formats and restore supported Bitcoin accounts; they are not reinterpreted as BIP39. Preserve any required original passphrase and compare known public addresses after import.

Private-key imports retain their network scope. Multisignature wallets retain their signer material and policy locally; support and required setup differ by chain. Keeping several signing keys on one device does not provide independent-device security. A wallet name or successful import does not establish that every previous account has been recovered.

Source: [mnemonic validation](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Import/OathMnemonicValidator.swift), [wallet engine](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathWalletEngine.swift), [private-key import](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathPrivateKeyImport.swift), and [multisignature creation](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathMultisigCreation.swift).

## Local storage and app lock

Wallet secrets are sealed in an authenticated AES-GCM vault, stored through non-synchronizing, device-only Keychain storage. An additional installation key is kept in a protected, backup-excluded app-container file. When enabled, the app passcode protects the vault key using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds. Biometrics and the selected auto-lock delay control access. Disabling the app passcode changes that protection; device compromise remains a risk.

Public wallet records, balances and history are stored separately in the local database. Removing the app also removes its installation key; do not treat reinstalling as a recovery method.

Source: [vault envelope](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathVaultEnvelope.swift), [vault storage](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathInstallationVaultStorage.swift), [installation protection](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathInstallationSecurity.swift), and [lock policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Security/OathSecurityPolicy.swift).

## Password-encrypted iCloud backup

For supported wallets, Oath creates a .oathbackup file encrypted on the device with AES-256-GCM. A separate backup password derives its key using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and a fresh 32-byte salt. Restore needs both that encrypted file and its password. The app passcode, a passkey, or Apple Account access alone cannot decrypt it.

Each eligible wallet has its own file. Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup in 4.1.14; preserve their original recovery words and required passphrase. Back Up All Wallets covers eligible active wallets, not Recently Deleted wallets. Verify each upload result. Existing iCloud files remain outside the local app-reset boundary.

Source: [backup format](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/Packages/OathCloudBackup/Sources/OathCloudBackup/BackupDocument.swift), [backup eligibility](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathWalletVault.swift), and [restore flow](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathCloudRestoreModel.swift). See the [backup guide](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/backup-password).

## Network and diagnostic boundaries

This source release has no operator endpoint for wallet credentials, recovery typing, wallet records or diagnostic uploads. Privacy-filtered diagnostics remain in a bounded local outbox. Blockchain providers still receive public queries for balances, fees and history, and signed transactions for broadcast. WalletConnect uses encrypted relay connections for user-approved sessions and signing requests. A signature, accepted broadcast and confirmed transaction are different outcomes.

Source: [local EVM signing](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Wallet/OathEVMSigning.swift), [send service](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Send/OathEVMSendService.swift), and [WalletConnect details](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/Documentation/WalletConnectReadableDetails.md).

## Copying recovery material

Explicit copies of recovery phrases, private keys and passphrases stay on the current device and expire from the system clipboard after 60 seconds. Information already pasted into another app is outside that expiry. Ordinary address and transaction-ID copies keep standard clipboard behavior. [Clipboard policy](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Shared/OathSensitiveClipboard.swift).

## Recovery limits

The 4.1.14 source does not provide Silent Payments receiving or discovery, the former nearby-iPhone transfer flow, or dice/coin/digit wallet creation. Its Bitcoin receive options depend on the imported material. Aezeed recovery covers supported on-chain Bitcoin branches, not Lightning channels or arbitrary custom LND accounts. Do not erase an older wallet until a supported recovery method reproduces its intended accounts. Never fund a public tutorial phrase or an example address.

Source: [import catalog](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/OathAtmosphere/Import/OathImportCatalog.swift), [Bitcoin keys](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/c21cc32c275b51f2a6c32af4475b279bde59c946/Packages/OathBitcoin/Sources/OathBitcoin/BitcoinKeys.swift), and [aezeed scope](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/blob/main/Packages/OathAezeed/README.md).

## Report a vulnerability

Use [GitHub private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/advisories/new). Include the affected version and reproduction steps using unfunded test material. Never send a real recovery phrase, private key, passphrase or backup password. Oath support cannot replace a missing recovery credential.


## Bug bounty

Help strengthen Oath through responsible security research. Our [bug bounty program](https://oathwallet.org/bug-bounty) defines scope, safe testing rules and rewards: Low $0, Medium $250, High $1,000 and Critical $10,000 for eligible, validated findings.

# Oath Wallet Bug Bounty

Program v1.0. Effective 2026-10-31.

Help us find vulnerabilities in Oath and make self-custody stronger for everyone.

[Report privately on GitHub](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/security/advisories/new). Private reporting is enabled; a GitHub account is required. Email alternative: care@oathwallet.org. Start with a non-sensitive summary.

## Rewards (USD)

### Low: $0

Limited security impact. Useful findings that strengthen the details.

Example: A narrowly constrained information exposure with no sensitive wallet data or meaningful privilege gain.

CVSS 0.1–3.9 (reference only).

### Medium: $250

A meaningful security weakness with limited impact or significant prerequisites.

Example: An exploitable access-control or application vulnerability affecting limited non-public data, without exposing signing keys or enabling unauthorized transfers.

CVSS 4.0–6.9 (reference only).

### High: $1,000

Substantial compromise of confidentiality, integrity or availability.

Example: A practical bypass of an important security boundary, significant sensitive-data exposure, or a serious signing flaw requiring constrained conditions.

CVSS 7.0–8.9 (reference only).

### Critical: $10,000

A direct, severe threat to wallet keys or user funds.

Example: A reproducible flaw that permits unauthorized signing, extraction of protected private keys, or irreversible loss of funds under realistic conditions. Demonstrate it only with test assets.

CVSS 9.0–10.0 (reference only).

[CVSS v4.0](https://www.first.org/cvss/v4.0/specification-document) is a reference, not an automatic payout calculation. Final severity considers demonstrated impact and the actual Oath exploit path.

## In scope

### Oath for iOS & iPadOS

The current publicly released Oath Wallet app. Include the exact app build, OS version and affected network. Focus on key protection, authentication, recovery, transaction construction and signing.

[View the app](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6780187283)

### Public source

Security-relevant Oath code in devdasx/oath-wallet. Pin the commit and demonstrate a reachable impact in a current supported feature. A source-only finding must identify the affected code and must not claim it proves App Store binary behavior.

[Explore the source](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet)

### Oath websites

Oath-controlled application behavior on oathwallet.org, help.oathwallet.org and articles.oathwallet.org. Use only your own account and test data. These exact hosts are in scope; other subdomains and infrastructure are not included automatically.

[Visit the website](https://oathwallet.org/)

## Out of scope

- Third-party wallets, dApps, blockchains, RPC providers, Apple, GitHub, cloud providers and other services are not authorized targets. A demonstrated vulnerability in Oath’s own use of a dependency can still qualify.
- Unverified scanner output, dependency version alerts, missing headers or best-practice recommendations without a reproducible security impact.
- Cosmetic issues, ordinary product bugs, unsupported features, price differences, market losses and service interruptions without an Oath security vulnerability.
- Expected behavior that requires the victim to disclose their recovery phrase, approve the accurately displayed malicious transaction, or grant the attacker full device control, unless a separate Oath security boundary is demonstrably bypassed.
- Issues already publicly documented, already known to Oath, or duplicate reports of the same root cause. Still report a materially different exploit path or an incomplete fix with new evidence.

## Testing rules

### Use a controlled environment

Use local builds, isolated forks or testnets with disposable wallets and synthetic data. Website testing must be non-destructive and limited to accounts and data you control. Do not use real user funds or send mainnet transactions to prove impact.

### Stop at the smallest proof

Do not access, copy, change or delete another person’s data. If you encounter it unexpectedly, stop immediately and report the minimum redacted evidence privately. Do not continue exploiting the issue or retain unnecessary data.

### Keep services available

No denial-of-service, stress tests, bulk scanning, brute force, spam, phishing, social engineering or physical attacks. Do not persist access, install malware, weaken protections or target staff, users or third-party infrastructure.

### Coordinate disclosure

Report promptly through the private channel. Keep exploit details private while we investigate and coordinate a disclosure date with us. Do not put vulnerabilities, secrets or personal data in public GitHub issues or social posts.

## Eligibility and payment

- Submit an original, reproducible security issue affecting an in-scope target. Explain the attacker’s prerequisites, the violated security boundary and the demonstrated impact.
- The first actionable report of a unique issue is eligible. Multiple symptoms of one root cause are assessed together, not paid separately. Findings from work already commissioned and paid for by Oath are not paid again under this program.
- Follow the testing rules and applicable law. If the ownership of a target or the safety of a test is unclear, ask before testing. This program does not authorize access to third-party systems.
- Oath validates the report and confirms its final severity with the researcher. Eligible accepted findings receive the listed USD reward for that severity; Low findings have no monetary reward. Informational reports are not paid. Submission alone does not establish eligibility.
- Payment arrangements and any necessary payment-compliance information are handled privately after acceptance. Do not include payment details or identity documents in the initial report. Oath will never ask for a payment, recovery phrase or private key to release a bounty.

## Review process

1. **Report privately:** Share the affected version, minimal reproduction and clear impact. Use the template below and redact sensitive information.
2. **Reproduce & assess:** We review scope, reproduce the issue and discuss severity. We may request a smaller proof or additional environment details.
3. **Resolve & reward:** We coordinate remediation, confirm eligibility and arrange the applicable reward privately. Response, fix and payment dates are confirmed in the report thread; no fixed turnaround is promised.
4. **Disclose together:** Agree on a safe publication date after remediation. Researcher credit is optional and requires your consent.

## Report template

[Download the report template](https://oathwallet.org/bug-bounty-report-template.txt). Do not include real wallet secrets or other people's data.

## Questions

### How is severity decided?

We assess demonstrated impact, exploitability, required privileges, user interaction and affected users. FIRST’s CVSS v4.0 ranges provide a reference, not an automatic payout calculation. Include a vector if helpful; Oath confirms the final category with an explanation. A theoretical maximum impact is not the same as a reproducible exploit.

### Do Low findings receive a reward?

Low findings have a $0 monetary reward. We still welcome actionable reports that improve Oath. Informational feedback is also welcome, but is not eligible for payment.

### Can I submit without a GitHub account?

Yes. Email care@oathwallet.org with the subject “Security report — Oath”. Start with a non-sensitive summary and ask for a private transfer route if your evidence needs one. Never send real recovery material, unredacted personal data or executable attachments.

### Can I test with a funded wallet?

Use a disposable wallet with no real funds. Demonstrate financial impact locally or on a testnet using test assets. Do not move, freeze or recover anyone else’s assets, even to prove a vulnerability.

### Is this a guarantee of legal immunity?

No. The permitted activities are limited to the scope and testing rules above. This page cannot authorize activity on third-party systems or waive another party’s rights. Ask us privately before any test whose authorization is unclear.

### What if my report is a duplicate or I disagree with the assessment?

We assess one root cause as one issue and use the first actionable submission. If you believe the assessment missed an exploit path or impact, reply in the private thread with the additional evidence. Do not create public issues containing exploit details.

### Does a bounty mean Oath has been independently audited?

No. This program invites vulnerability research; it is not an independent security audit, a certification, or a guarantee that software has no vulnerabilities.

### What if the program changes?

The published scope and rewards may be updated prospectively. We assess a report using the program version in effect when it was received. This page identifies its version and effective date so researchers can reference them.

# Privacy Policy

Last updated: October 30, 2026

**In short:** No account signup, email or KYC is required to use the wallet. You control the wallet credentials. The App Store version of Oath Wallet does not send us app analytics or automatic error reports. Optional encrypted backups, deliberate exports, WalletConnect and network services and the website's separate features have the data boundaries described below. We do not sell personal data or share it for cross-context behavioural advertising.

## 1. Who we are

This Privacy Policy explains how STAGE AND STYLE COLLECTIVE LLC, 2103 Condor Ct, Redmond, Oregon 97756-8281, United States (“Oath”, “we”, “us”) handles personal data when you use Oath Wallet distributed through the App Store and the Oath website (the “Service”). We are the data controller for the limited personal data described here.

Contact: care@oathwallet.org.

## 2. Our approach

The App Store app does not collect user analytics or automatically upload error reports. Network requests, optional services, website visits and information you choose to send us are described separately below. We do not require an account, name, email address, phone number or identity documents to use the wallet app or browse the website. The optional newsletter requires an email address.

## 3. Wallet credentials and device storage

In the 4.1.14 public source, recovery material is sealed in an authenticated local vault using device-only Keychain storage and an additional installation key in the protected app container. Public wallet metadata and transaction records are stored separately in the local database. Signing takes place locally; network providers receive public queries and signed transactions, not the spending credentials used to sign them.

Optional encrypted iCloud backup can store eligible wallet material at your request. Manual export can also reveal or copy recovery material under your control. Do not interpret on-device storage as a promise that a user-authorized export never leaves the device.

Explicit copies of recovery phrases, private keys and passphrases stay on the current device and expire from the system clipboard after 60 seconds. Information already pasted into another app is outside that expiry.

Face ID and Touch ID are handled by iOS; Oath does not receive your biometric templates. Public source publication does not independently establish a match to a distributed App Store binary. See [the security evidence and version scope](https://oathwallet.org/security).

## 4. Password-encrypted backup and WalletConnect

Optional iCloud backup encrypts an eligible wallet on the device with AES-256-GCM. Its key is derived from a separate backup password using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 600,000 rounds and a fresh salt. Restore requires both the encrypted backup file and its backup password. Oath does not receive the password or a plaintext backup. Apple operates iCloud Drive under its own policies.

Electrum and aezeed wallets are not eligible for iCloud backup in 4.1.14; preserve their original recovery material. Existing backup files remain outside the app-reset boundary. The former passkey-based backup and nearby-iPhone transfer flows are not current recovery methods. Keep an older device until a supported recovery method is verified.

WalletConnect uses encrypted relay connections to pair with a dApp. A user-approved connection can share public accounts and requested signatures or signed transactions with that dApp. It does not send recovery phrases or private keys. Review the destination and request before approving.

## 5. Data processed to provide the Service

To show balances, prices and history and to broadcast transactions, the app connects to blockchain nodes and price-data services. These requests can reveal:

- Your public wallet addresses and transactions (which are public on blockchains by design)
- Your device’s IP address and basic technical information (such as app version and device type)
- Your chosen display currency and language

## Notification services in earlier releases

The 4.1.14 public source does not register wallet addresses or notification tokens with an operator notification service. Earlier releases and separately enabled services may have registered public wallet information, notification tokens and device metadata. Contact us about data you previously supplied to those services; updating the app alone does not delete earlier service records.

## Website visitor statistics

On oathwallet.org, we use first-party website analytics to understand visits and App Store download-button clicks. A random, first-party browser identifier is stored in a Secure, HttpOnly cookie for up to one year. Session information in your browser groups activity into visits after 30 minutes of inactivity. We record page paths (not query strings), referral domains (not full referral URLs), broad browser/device categories, and approximate country/city and rounded coordinates derived by Cloudflare from your IP address. This is not GPS location and does not request device-location access. Our analytics records do not store your raw IP address or link visits to wallet data.

Restricted administrators can view statistics, anonymous returning-browser history, and visit/download alerts in the restricted administration console. Detailed events are retained for up to 400 days. Clearing the cookie creates a new anonymous browser identity. We exclude detected automated traffic and honour Global Privacy Control and Do Not Track signals. You can enable those browser settings to opt out of this website analytics. Download clicks are not evidence of app installation.


## Optional Oath Notes newsletter

If you choose to subscribe, we store your email address, selected topics, signup source page, consent version and timestamps, subscription status and signup method, and subscription changes to provide the newsletter. Newsletter signup is optional and is not connected to wallet addresses, balances, recovery phrases, or private keys. Submitting the signup form subscribes you immediately; no email confirmation is required. Emails may include Oath Wallet releases, crypto news and market prices, security alerts, and practical guides.

Our email delivery provider processes the recipient address and message content. We record sending, delivery, bounce, complaint, and unsubscribe events. When engagement measurement is enabled for a campaign, tracking pixels and redirect links can report opens and clicks. These are approximate signals: email privacy services and security scanners may create events without a person reading or clicking. We do not store the IP addresses or user-agent strings received in newsletter event reports.

You can change topics or unsubscribe using the private link in an email. Unsubscribed addresses and permanent delivery failures are suppressed from future campaigns. We retain subscription and consent records while needed to deliver the newsletter, honour opt-outs, and resolve delivery or abuse issues. Contact care@oathwallet.org to request access or deletion; a minimal suppression record may be retained to prevent future unwanted messages.

The website remembers that the signup dialog appeared using browser local storage and a preference cookie (up to 400 days). This preference does not identify you and is not linked to subscriber records. It stops repeated prompts in that browser. Clearing browser storage, private browsing, or using another device can show the dialog again. Short-lived, keyed IP hashes help limit automated signup and login attempts; raw IP addresses are not saved in the newsletter database.

## 6. App analytics and error reports

The App Store version of Oath Wallet does not automatically upload app errors, crash reports, usage analytics or diagnostic logs to our servers. Website visitor statistics and information you voluntarily send to support are separate from the app and are described in this policy.

If you choose to share analytics with app developers in iOS settings, Apple may provide us with aggregated crash reports and performance data that do not identify you. You can change this at any time in Settings › Privacy & Security › Analytics & Improvements.

## 7. Support requests

If you contact care@oathwallet.org, we process your email address and the contents of your message to respond. Never include your recovery phrase or private keys.

## 8. Why we process data (legal bases)

Where laws such as the EU/UK GDPR apply, we rely on:

- Performance of a contract — to provide the Service you request (connecting to networks, showing prices)
- Legitimate interests — to keep the Service secure, prevent abuse and fix bugs, balanced against your rights
- Consent — for the optional newsletter, which you can withdraw at any time
- Legal obligation — where we must comply with applicable law

## 9. What we don’t do

We do not sell personal data, “share” it for cross-context behavioural advertising, build advertising profiles, use third-party ad trackers, or make decisions about you based solely on automated processing that produce legal effects.

## 10. Sharing with service providers

We may use a small number of service providers (such as blockchain node providers, price-data providers, hosting and email providers) who process data on our behalf under written contracts that require confidentiality and security. We may disclose information where required by law or to protect rights and safety, and we will resist over-broad requests where the law allows.

## 11. International transfers

Our providers may process data in countries other than yours. Where required, we protect transfers with appropriate safeguards such as the European Commission’s Standard Contractual Clauses, the UK International Data Transfer Addendum, or other lawful transfer mechanisms.

## 12. Retention

Network and price requests are not stored by us beyond what our providers need for security logs (typically no longer than 30 days). Support emails are kept only as long as needed to resolve your request, then deleted, unless we must keep them by law.

## 13. Security

The published source uses device-only Keychain storage, local signing, authenticated encryption for the local vault and optional iCloud backup, and encrypted network connections. Blockchain private keys are not described as Secure Enclave signing keys. The version-specific evidence and limitations are documented at https://oathwallet.org/security; published source is available at https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet.

## 14. Your rights

Depending on where you live, you may have the right to access, correct, delete or port your personal data, to object to or restrict processing, and to withdraw consent. Removing the app removes its installation key, but does not delete separate iCloud backups or earlier service records; use the deletion methods described below. To exercise any right, email care@oathwallet.org. We will respond within the time required by law and will not discriminate against you for exercising your rights.

You also have the right to complain to your local data-protection authority.

## 15. Regional information

We aim to meet the requirements of privacy laws worldwide, including:

- European Union, EEA and United Kingdom — GDPR and UK GDPR
- United States — CCPA/CPRA (California) and other state privacy laws; we honour Global Privacy Control signals, and we do not sell or share personal information
- Brazil — LGPD
- Canada — PIPEDA and applicable provincial laws
- Australia — Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles
- Japan — APPI · South Korea — PIPA · Singapore — PDPA · Thailand — PDPA
- India — Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023
- China — PIPL
- Saudi Arabia — PDPL · United Arab Emirates — PDPL · Türkiye — KVKK
- South Africa — POPIA · Nigeria — NDPA · Kenya — Data Protection Act

## 16. Children

The Service is not directed to children under 13 (or under 16 where required by local law), and we do not knowingly collect their personal data. If you believe a child has contacted us, email care@oathwallet.org and we will delete the information.

## 17. Deleting your data

Use the app’s wallet-removal or reset controls for their supported local deletion scope, and verify your independent recovery material first. Deleting the app alone does not guarantee removal of Keychain items. iCloud backups are outside the app-reset boundary and must be managed separately through your iCloud storage. Assets remain on their blockchains; future access depends on retaining the correct recovery material and any required passphrase or output-specific information. To delete support correspondence, email care@oathwallet.org from the address you used.

## 18. Changes to this policy

We will post any changes here and update the “Last updated” date. For material changes, we will notify you in the app before they take effect.

Questions: care@oathwallet.org

# Create your first wallet

Start with a new wallet, then give it a name and color you recognize.

A newly created recovery-phrase wallet has new keys and addresses. Choosing a familiar name does not restore an older wallet; use Import or Restore for that.

Keep the recovery phrase and any additional passphrase independently of the app passcode. Before funding, verify that you have a usable recovery route.

Verify the wallet name and intended public address after setup. A newly generated wallet and an imported wallet can have the same label while controlling different accounts.

The welcome options and wallet-management flow also offer supported multisignature creation. Choose the chain and signer policy shown by the app; activation and funding requirements vary by chain. Keeping every signer on this phone does not create separate-device protection.

## Steps

1. On Welcome, choose Create a new wallet. To restore an existing wallet instead, choose Import wallet or Restore from iCloud.
2. Create a six-digit app passcode and enter it again to confirm. Complete biometric setup if offered and desired.
3. On Customize Wallet, enter a recognizable name and choose a color. Tap Continue to open the wallet.
4. Check the wallet name on Home, then open Receive for the network you intend to use. Do not fund an example address from a help screenshot.
5. Open the wallet’s settings and make a recovery backup before receiving funds. Keep the recovery phrase and any passphrase separately from the phone.
6. Return to Home and allow balances and activity to refresh. A brand-new wallet can correctly show no activity and zero balances.

A new wallet is different from importing an existing one. Your app passcode unlocks Oath; it is not a recovery phrase or backup password.

# Import a recovery phrase

Bring an existing wallet into Oath using supported BIP39, Electrum or aezeed recovery words and any required passphrase.

Import reconstructs supported accounts from the phrase; it does not move coins on-chain. Enter the original order and language, and never replace an invalid word by guessing.

A separate BIP-39 passphrase creates different accounts. If your previous wallet used one, restore that exact passphrase wallet and compare addresses before concluding a balance is missing.

Verify the wallet name and intended public address after setup. A newly generated wallet and an imported wallet can have the same label while controlling different accounts.

BIP39, Electrum and aezeed are different recovery formats. Use the format recognized by the import screen and enter the original seed extension or aezeed password when requested. Electrum and aezeed imports are Bitcoin-only; aezeed does not restore Lightning channels or arbitrary custom LND accounts.

Electrum and aezeed wallets are not eligible for iCloud backup in 4.1.14. Keep their original words and required passphrase or password independently.

## Steps

1. Tap Import wallet. If you already use Oath, open Settings → Wallets → Import wallet.
2. Enter the words in their original order, use Paste, or use the scan button for a compatible recovery QR.
3. Review any word-count, unknown-word or checksum message. Correct the original phrase rather than guessing new words.
4. Tap Import. On first setup, create and confirm your app passcode. Name and customize the wallet, then tap Continue.
5. After import, open Receive on the original network and compare the full public address with your previous wallet. Use a supported address/path choice if the original account requires it.
6. Wait for balances and history to refresh. If an address differs, check recovery language, word order, additional passphrase and supported account rules; importing a valid phrase alone does not prove it is the intended account.

Never enter recovery words into this website, a support message, or an online checker. A wallet protected by a BIP-39 passphrase also needs that exact passphrase.

# Scan a recovery-phrase QR code

Use the camera to import a compatible recovery phrase without typing every word.

A recovery QR contains secret material. Scan it privately from a source you control, not from a public website or a person offering support.

The import validation still applies after scanning. A recognized QR is not proof that the wallet belongs to you or has a trustworthy history.

Verify the wallet name and intended public address after setup. A newly generated wallet and an imported wallet can have the same label while controlling different accounts.

## Steps

1. Open Import wallet and tap the scan icon in the navigation bar.
2. Allow camera access when iOS asks. Point the camera at a recovery QR you trust.
3. After a recognized phrase fills the field, review validation and tap Import.
4. If camera access was denied, use Open Settings in the error message, enable Camera for Oath and try again.

A receiving-address QR is not a recovery phrase. Do not share or photograph recovery QR codes.

# Import a private key

Import the key for a particular network or the shared Ethereum & EVM group.

A private-key wallet usually restores one key or a supported scoped account, not all accounts generated by a recovery phrase. Choose the import type that matches your original recovery material.

Review the address after import. A valid key in the wrong network or derivation context can show an account you did not intend.

Verify the wallet name and intended public address after setup. A newly generated wallet and an imported wallet can have the same label while controlling different accounts.

## Steps

1. Open Import private key from the welcome options or Settings → Wallets.
2. Choose the network. Ethereum & EVM groups the supported EVM networks into one import choice.
3. Enter or paste the private key in the format expected by that network. Review the validation result.
4. Confirm the import, complete first-time passcode setup if asked, then customize the wallet.
5. Open Receive for the chosen network and compare the full address with the original account. Do not rely only on its nickname or logo.
6. Keep the original key or a verified encrypted backup. Allow fresh network data to load; importing does not transfer any funds on-chain.

A private-key wallet does not have a recovery phrase in Oath. Keep the original key or an encrypted backup. A single private key and an extended HD key are not the same kind of recovery material.

# Which private-key formats can I import?

Choose the correct network before entering key material. Oath validates both format and key structure.

Do not convert formats by manually trimming characters or discarding bytes. Use the original supported export and correct network choice.

If Oath rejects a format, stop and identify the original wallet’s export type. A public address, extended public key or keystore password alone is not a private key.

Verify the wallet name and intended public address after setup. A newly generated wallet and an imported wallet can have the same label while controlling different accounts.

## Steps

1. For Bitcoin-family networks, use the supported WIF, raw key or extended private-key form for that network. An account-scoped extended key only recovers the addresses within its scope.
2. For Ethereum & EVM or TRON, use a 32-byte hexadecimal key. Solana accepts its Base58 keypair or a JSON byte-array keypair.
3. NEAR expects an ed25519: keypair; Stellar uses an S-prefixed secret StrKey. Sui uses an Ed25519 suiprivkey value.
4. Aptos accepts an Ed25519 hexadecimal or AIP-80 key. XRP Ledger uses a supported secp256k1 key; Gram uses a supported Ed25519 hexadecimal key.

Do not convert keys on an unfamiliar website. A public address, xpub, or transaction ID is not a private key. Other signature schemes or wallet-specific export formats may not import.

The six-digit app passcode protects local wallet access; it is not the recovery phrase or your iCloud backup password.

# Find your way around Home

Use the Wallet, History and Search icons, and find the controls for your active wallet.

Wallet, History and Search are different views of the same active wallet. Selecting the Wallet navigation icon returns to Home. The name capsule in the top toolbar opens the wallet switcher.

Search follows the last section you selected: Wallet searches assets, while History searches transactions. Select the section you want before opening Search.

For the main Settings screen, return to the top of Home until the sliders icon is visible. Currency, Language and Appearance are directly in Settings; there is no separate Preferences screen.

A long wallet name stays on one line and ends with an ellipsis inside the capsule. VoiceOver reads the full name. The wallet’s saved name is not shortened or changed.

## Steps

1. Open the Wallet tab to see the active wallet’s total and Assets list.
2. Use the wallet-name capsule in the top toolbar to switch wallets. The adjacent sliders action opens Settings; the scanner opens the shared QR scanner.
3. Read the balance-change capsule under the total as an observed change in this wallet’s value. It is not a profit report or a button for a balance-history chart.
4. Tap Send or Receive for a transfer flow. Tap an asset for its price, actions and activity.
5. Select Wallet and then the separate Search icon to search assets, including an exact contract or mint address.
6. Open History for transactions across the active wallet. Pull down from the top to refresh; cached information can remain visible while newer data arrives.

The total is a valuation based on available balances, prices and exchange rates. Missing or delayed provider data can affect it. Check the actual asset quantity and network when reviewing a transfer.

# Switch wallets from Home

Use the glass name capsule above your balance to select another wallet or add one.

The name capsule and balance are separate buttons. Tapping the capsule opens the switcher; tapping the large amount hides or reveals balances.

Long names are shortened visually with an ellipsis so the capsule remains on one line. Open the switcher to identify the wallet, or use VoiceOver to hear the complete name. The saved wallet name is unchanged.

Switching changes the active wallet used by Home and History. Asset navigation, searches and history filters reset for the newly selected wallet so they do not keep showing results from the previous one.

Creating or importing a wallet continues through the existing setup and customization flow. Phrase and private-key import open after the switcher closes. Restore from iCloud opens its backup list in the sheet.

Use the sliders icon for app settings and the wallet-colored toolbar shortcut after scrolling for current-wallet settings. Settings → Wallets still opens management; its rows are separate from the Home switcher.

3. Tap its row and wait for Home to load that wallet. Read the name in the toolbar before continuing.
4. Open Receive and compare the public address for the intended network, especially when two wallets have similar names.
5. To add another wallet, use the create, import, private-key import or iCloud restore actions in the switcher or Settings → Wallets.

Switching wallets does not transfer funds. A wallet-row valuation can use cached balances and prices; it is not a guarantee of a fresh network check.

# Reorder your wallets

Put frequently used wallets where you want them in the list.

The checkmark in the top bar is an action that finishes editing. The small check attached to a wallet’s icon is a selection badge; it is not a second Done button.

Reordering changes the wallet list only. It does not change the order of assets or move funds between wallets.

Reordering changes the list order, not the active wallet or its keys. The check badge identifies selection independently of position.

Use the native editing handles and finish with the toolbar checkmark so the list exits editing mode.

## Steps

1. Open Settings → Wallets and tap Edit.
2. Drag a wallet by its reorder handle to the position you want.
3. Repeat as needed, then tap the native checkmark in the top bar to finish editing.
4. Reopen Wallets to see the saved order. The check badge on a wallet icon still identifies the active wallet.

This changes wallet order. Asset lists are sorted by portfolio value and activity, not by this setting.

# Move a wallet to Recently Deleted

Remove a wallet from the active list while keeping a short recovery window.

For an ordinary removal while other active wallets remain, the wallet enters Recently Deleted for seven days. This affects the local app, not funds or token approvals on the blockchain.

Removing the final active wallet instead follows a reset flow. If Recently Deleted contains wallets, Oath asks you to permanently remove those first. Cancel if you do not have recovery material for them.

After the final active wallet is removed, Oath returns to Welcome. Existing iCloud files are separate from the local deletion; protect their passwords and remove cloud copies separately only if that is your intention.

## Steps

1. Tap Edit and use the remove control for the wallet.
2. Authenticate with enabled biometrics or your app passcode when requested.
3. Read the native confirmation dialog and confirm removal.
4. Find the removed wallet under Recently Deleted in the Wallets screen.

Removed wallets are retained for seven days before automatic cleanup. Removing a wallet does not move on-chain funds or delete an existing iCloud backup. Keep a separate backup before removal.

# Recover a recently deleted wallet

Bring a wallet back before its retention window expires.

Removed wallets normally remain recoverable locally for seven days. Each row shows its own deadline; expired items are permanently removed the next time Oath is unlocked.

Restore returns the retained wallet to the active list. If it was permanently deleted, use its original recovery material or encrypted iCloud backup instead.

Removing the final active wallet is a different flow: it requires clearing Recently Deleted and then resets the local app.

## Steps

1. Open Settings → Wallets → Recently Deleted before the displayed deletion deadline.
2. Select the wallets to restore. Use Select All or Deselect All to change the selection.
3. Tap Restore. Complete authentication if requested and wait for the operation to finish.
4. Return to Wallets, choose the restored wallet and check its receiving address and refreshed assets.

Each row shows when removal becomes permanent. Do not rely on Recently Deleted as your only backup.

# Permanently delete removed wallets

Clear wallets from Recently Deleted when you no longer need their local copies.

Return to Wallets and confirm the intended wallet and active selection. A local management action does not itself transfer funds or change network permissions.

The displayed deletion deadline is a remaining local recovery window, not a blockchain expiry. Permanent deletion closes that local recovery route immediately.

Read the selected count and names again at confirmation. If you are uncertain about a backup, cancel and restore the wallet first so you can verify its recovery options.

## Steps

1. Open Recently Deleted and select the wallets you intend to erase. Compare their names and deletion dates.
2. Check that you have an independently usable recovery phrase, private key or encrypted backup for anything you may need later.
3. Tap Delete Permanently, the destructive secondary button below Restore.
4. Read the confirmation and authenticate if requested. Confirm only the selected wallets you intend to erase.
5. After completion, verify those rows are gone. A permanently deleted wallet cannot be restored from Recently Deleted.

Permanent deletion cannot be undone using Recently Deleted. Existing external backups and on-chain records are separate.

# Create a wallet with a BIP-39 passphrase

Derive a separate wallet from the same recovery phrase plus an exact passphrase.

The additional BIP-39 passphrase is part of the key derivation. Every different value, including differences in case or spaces, produces a different wallet.

It is not the app passcode and not an iCloud encryption password. Record the exact phrase and passphrase together in a secure recovery plan; the passphrase wallet needs its own verification and backup.

Return to Wallets and confirm the intended wallet and active selection. A local management action does not itself transfer funds or change network permissions.

For supported Electrum seeds, a seed extension follows Electrum rules rather than BIP39 rules. Preserve the exact original recovery format. Private-key, multisignature and aezeed wallets do not offer the BIP39 Add Passphrase flow.

## Steps

1. Choose a recovery-phrase wallet and tap Add Passphrase.
2. Read the explanation and continue.
3. Enter the passphrase and its confirmation exactly, including capitalization and spaces. Use the eye control to check your entry privately.
4. Create the wallet, then choose its name and color. Back up the new passphrase wallet too.

This does not add a password to the existing wallet. Every different passphrase produces a different wallet; you need both the recovery phrase and that exact passphrase to recover it. The option is not available for private-key wallets.

# Back up all wallets to iCloud

Start an encrypted backup for every active wallet from one screen.

The backup flow encrypts the supported wallet material before saving backup files to your iCloud Drive. The backup password is required to restore those files.

Check each wallet’s outcome. A batch can contain a failed upload even when another wallet completed; retain an independent recovery copy until the relevant upload is confirmed.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

In 4.1.14, Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup. Preserve their original recovery material. Back Up All Wallets processes eligible active wallets; it excludes Recently Deleted wallets.

## Steps

1. Tap Back Up All Wallets.
2. Choose a backup password of at least eight characters and confirm it. Keep it somewhere safe.
3. Tap Back Up and keep Oath open while it prepares the encrypted wallet files.
4. Check every wallet’s status. Preparation or uploading is not the same as a completed backup.

Each wallet has its own encrypted backup file, using the password you just chose. Recently Deleted wallets are excluded. Restore these files individually. Your app passcode does not replace the backup password.

# Back up one wallet to iCloud

Create an encrypted recovery file for a particular wallet.

Select the wallet by name before enabling its backup. A backup for one wallet is not automatically a backup for every other wallet in the app.

Keep Oath open until its upload status completes. If iCloud is unavailable, fix the account, Drive, storage or connectivity issue and retry.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

In 4.1.14, Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup. Preserve their original recovery material. Back Up All Wallets processes eligible active wallets; it excludes Recently Deleted wallets.

## Steps

1. Open the wallet’s settings and turn on Back Up to iCloud.
2. Enter and confirm a backup password with at least eight characters.
3. Tap Back Up, then wait for the upload status to complete.
4. Keep the password safe; the app cannot recover a forgotten backup password.

Files are stored in iCloud Drive → Oath Wallet → Wallet Backups. Turning off the switch keeps existing files in iCloud Drive.

# Understand your backup password

The password for an iCloud backup is separate from your app passcode and BIP-39 passphrase.

Choose a backup password you can recover without access to this phone. It is separate from the six-digit app passcode.

Oath cannot decrypt an existing file with a newly chosen password. Keep the password that was used for each backup file you retain.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

## Steps

1. Choose a password of at least eight characters that you can recover independently.
2. Enter it twice and use the eye controls to review the fields privately.
3. Use that password when restoring the corresponding backup file.
4. If you create another backup with a different password, retain the correct password for each file you keep.

Oath cannot reset the password of an encrypted backup. If you still have an accessible wallet, create a new backup with a password you know.

# Restore from an iCloud backup

Recover a wallet from an encrypted Oath backup file.

Restoring downloads an encrypted file and requires its own backup password. Signing into the correct Apple Account alone is not sufficient to decrypt it.

After restoration, compare the wallet name and public addresses with the original. Network balances and transaction history are fetched separately; allow refresh to finish.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

In 4.1.14, Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup. Preserve their original recovery material. Back Up All Wallets processes eligible active wallets; it excludes Recently Deleted wallets.

## Steps

1. Sign in to the Apple Account that holds the backup and enable iCloud Drive.
2. Choose Restore from iCloud under Welcome’s more options, in Home’s wallet-name capsule switcher, or under Settings → Wallets.
3. Select a backup by its displayed date and enter that file’s backup password.
4. Wait while Oath downloads, decrypts and saves the wallet. Finish customization when shown.

An all-wallet backup creates separate files; restore them individually with the correct backup password. A passkey or the app passcode does not decrypt a .oathbackup file.

# Check whether a backup has finished

Read the per-wallet result instead of assuming a switched-on toggle means success.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

Preparing means Oath is constructing the encrypted backup. Uploading means the cloud operation is still in progress. An error or unavailable state must not be counted as a completed backup.

Review the status for each wallet you intend to preserve. Keep its backup password and any recovery passphrase independently; a successful upload alone does not mean you remember how to decrypt it.

In 4.1.14, Electrum and aezeed wallets are excluded from iCloud backup. Preserve their original recovery material. Back Up All Wallets processes eligible active wallets; it excludes Recently Deleted wallets.

## Steps

1. Open Backup to see every active wallet’s state.
2. Wait for preparation and uploading to finish.
3. If a wallet shows a failure, read its message and use Try Again.
4. Only treat the backup as complete after iCloud confirms the upload.

Closing or locking the app can interrupt preparation of remaining wallets. Encrypted jobs already saved to the upload queue can resume. Review the individual results after returning.

# Fix an iCloud backup or restore problem

Check the Apple Account, storage and backup file before retrying.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

A simulator without an Apple Account shows the unavailable state illustrated here. The screenshot is not evidence that a file was uploaded or restored.

If the backup is listed but will not decrypt, check the password for that specific file. Changing the app passcode does not change an old backup file’s encryption password.

## Steps

1. Check your internet connection and that iCloud Drive is enabled for the Apple Account you intend to use.
2. Check available iCloud storage. Free space if a quota error appears.
3. For restore, confirm that the file is in iCloud Drive → Oath Wallet → Wallet Backups and that its password is correct.
4. Return to Oath and tap Try Again. If the account changed during the operation, restart it with the intended account.

Do not delete the app or the only backup file to troubleshoot. Contact support with the error text, never your recovery phrase, private key or backup password.

# View your recovery phrase

Open the recovery words for a phrase-based wallet when you need an offline backup.

Anyone with the full recovery phrase and any required passphrase can control the wallet. View it only in a private place and do not send it to support.

The screenshots in this guide deliberately stop at the protective screen. They never show a populated recovery phrase.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

Recovery phrases, private keys and passphrases copied in Oath stay on this device and expire from the system clipboard after 60 seconds. They are not shared through Universal Clipboard. Public addresses and transaction identifiers keep ordinary copy behavior. Copy only when needed; expiry cannot remove information you have already pasted into another app.

## Steps

1. Choose the correct wallet and tap View Recovery Phrase.
2. Read the warning in a private place and acknowledge it.
3. Complete the requested authentication.
4. Write down the words in their displayed order and keep them offline. Leave the screen when finished.

Never share the words with support, websites or other people. Avoid screenshots. Private-key imports do not have a recovery phrase to display. For a passphrase wallet, recovery also requires the exact BIP-39 passphrase.

# Restore your wallets on another iPhone

Use recovery material or an encrypted iCloud backup before removing the old installation.

Treat the backup as usable only when the relevant operation has completed and you retain the correct recovery material or file password. Loading, preparing and unavailable states are not successful backups.

Import or restore each distinct wallet, not only the wallet that happened to be active. Preserve names, any added BIP-39 passphrases and supported address/path choices needed to recognize the same accounts.

Wait for data refresh, then compare full public addresses on the same network. A matching nickname or a nonzero balance is not sufficient evidence that every old account was restored.

## Steps

1. On the old phone, confirm each wallet has a usable recovery backup and retain any required passphrase or backup password.
2. On the new phone, open Oath and choose Import wallet, Import private key, or Restore from iCloud.
3. Complete setup and compare receiving addresses for the same network and derivation path.
4. Check all wallets before deleting any local copy on the old phone.

The current build does not offer a direct phone-to-phone transfer flow. Deleting and reinstalling the app requires recovery; the app passcode alone is insufficient.

# Unlock Oath

Use your app passcode or enabled biometrics to open the app.

An incorrect code produces an inline message and red passcode dots, with a shake and error haptic where device settings allow them. There is no incorrect-passcode dialog to dismiss; wait for the entry to reset and try again.

Reduce Motion can suppress the shake. Haptic feedback depends on the device and system settings; the visible error remains available.

The keypad keeps its normal appearance while a biometric prompt is active. Complete or dismiss that prompt before continuing with a passcode. Authentication is still required even when the keys do not look dimmed.

## Steps

1. Enter your six-digit app passcode, or complete Face ID or Touch ID when offered.
2. If automatic biometric authentication is canceled, use the keypad or the biometric icon.
3. If a passcode is incorrect, the dots turn red with an inline error. Try again carefully.
4. If Oath asks you to wait after repeated failures, wait before another attempt.

The keypad passcode is the one created in Oath. It is not necessarily your iPhone’s device passcode.

Require authentication to enter Oath.

Control how long Oath stays unlocked after moving to the background.
