# What if I forget my app passcode?

Keep recovery options separate from the app lock.

Oath support cannot tell you your passcode or reconstruct a missing recovery phrase. Resetting the app is not a way to bypass decryption of the existing vault.

Do not remove the app or its final wallet while it holds your only usable recovery copy. Preserve the device and seek guidance using nonsecret information.

Review the resulting security setting before leaving. Public account activity remains visible on-chain even when the app is locked or its balance display is hidden.

## Steps

1. If biometric unlock still works, use it to access the app and make sure your recovery backups are available.
2. Locate your recovery phrase, private key or encrypted iCloud backup and its password. Include the BIP-39 passphrase for any passphrase wallet.
3. Do not delete Oath until you have verified a usable recovery route.
4. If needed, ask support for guidance without sending any secret recovery material.

There is no email reset that recovers your wallet from the six-digit app passcode. Reinstalling the app destroys access to its previous local installation keys.

# Understand balances and portfolio value

Oath shows token quantities and a local-currency valuation.

The smaller quantity underneath an asset name is measured in that coin or token, such as BTC or USDT. The value on the opposite side is its conversion into the selected display currency.

The app may shorten a very long quantity to keep list rows readable. Open the asset or its public explorer to inspect more detail; display formatting does not change the balance.

Wallet-list values use available saved balances and market data. A total does not include a reliable valuation for an asset when a required price or exchange rate is missing.

## Steps

1. Read the total at the top for the active wallet’s available valuation.
2. In each row, read the native quantity under the asset name and the local-currency amount on the opposite side.
3. Open an asset for a closer view.
4. If a value looks stale, refresh and compare the exact account and network in an explorer.

A local-currency value uses available prices and exchange rates; it is not a sale quote. A displayed zero is not proof that a network query succeeded or that an asset has no market value.

# Refresh balances and activity

Request updated data without leaving your wallet.

Pull-to-refresh belongs to the native scroll view. The Oath logo animates in the refresh area while the current content remains available.

Refresh requests updated balances and available activity; it does not send funds or guarantee a provider has indexed a just-broadcast transaction. An unchanged result can be correct.

If refresh fails, retain the transaction ID and compare the same network in its explorer. Check the active wallet, any asset/history filters and connectivity before repeating.

## Steps

1. Scroll to the top of Home or the asset screen.
2. Pull down and release to start a refresh.
3. Wait for the Oath refresh animation to complete.
4. If data has not changed, check your connection and try again later.

Providers can return delayed or incomplete data. Oath retains cached information when updates fail; a refresh is not confirmation that a pending transfer has settled.

# Find and add a token by address

Look up a supported contract or mint address and review its details before adding it.

Manual lookup is available for the supported EVM networks, TRON and Solana. The same-looking address or symbol on a different network is a different token.

Explicitly tracking a token can make otherwise unlisted token activity visible. It does not certify the token as legitimate, obtain a market price, or override identified phishing metadata and blocked-token protection.

Quantity, market price, logo and transaction history are separate data. An unavailable quote or delayed provider response does not by itself establish that an asset balance is zero.

## Steps

1. Tap Wallet, then the magnifying-glass Search icon. Paste the exact token contract address, or Solana mint address.
2. Wait for lookup on supported networks present in the active wallet. If some lookups fail, use Try Again for an incomplete result.
3. Tap a result and review its network, full address, name, symbol, standard and decimals.
4. Compare the full token identity with information you obtained independently from the project, then tap Add Token.
5. After addition succeeds, tap the native checkmark to finish. Oath tracks the token for that account.

Manual address lookup supports the app’s EVM networks, TRON and Solana. Results can be incomplete if a provider fails. Adding a token does not buy it, approve it or transfer funds.

# Why isn’t a token appearing?

Check the wallet, network, address and lookup result before assuming funds are missing.

Filtering affects what Oath displays; it does not destroy a token balance or undo an on-chain transfer. A genuine new token can be absent from verification lists.

An asset can also have a quantity but no available local-currency price. Missing price coverage and missing balance data are different problems.

Quantity, market price, logo and transaction history are separate data. An unavailable quote or delayed provider response does not by itself establish that an asset balance is zero.

## Steps

1. Check the active-wallet badge in Settings → Wallets. For Solana, also check the selected path in Receive.
2. Confirm the sender’s exact network and account, then inspect the transaction in that network’s explorer.
3. Consider whether verification or spam filtering is hiding the token. A familiar ticker or a price is not enough to establish its identity.
4. For a token you independently recognize on a supported manual-lookup network, select Wallet → Search and paste its exact contract or mint address.
5. If lookup is incomplete, retry after checking your connection. If the mismatch remains, send support the public network and transaction ID, never recovery material.

Some automatically discovered tokens are filtered using provider verification lists. An unsupported price, filtered token or failed request does not erase a blockchain holding.

# How assets are sorted

The list prioritizes portfolio value instead of alphabetical order alone.

Quantity, market price, logo and transaction history are separate data. An unavailable quote or delayed provider response does not by itself establish that an asset balance is zero.

Price availability can change the ordering: an asset without a usable quote may not sit beside similarly valuable priced assets. Sorting is not a safety or authenticity rating.

Use the active filters and Search to find assets intentionally; an asset moving down the list does not mean it was sold or removed.

## Steps

1. Look near the top for assets with the highest available local-currency value.
2. Assets with equal values are ordered by transaction activity, then name and a stable tie-break.
3. Use search to find a low-value or zero-value asset quickly.
4. Refresh to update the values used in ordering.

This order is automatic. Reordering wallets does not reorder the assets inside them.

# Read an asset’s price and chart

View the latest available market quote and its recent movement.

A quote and a chart are separate pieces of market data. Having a price does not guarantee a 24-hour chart, and an absent chart control does not mean that the token cannot exist or has no value.

The timestamp helps you judge freshness even though provider and cache labels are hidden. Previously saved data can remain visible when a refresh cannot obtain new data.

Quantity, market price, logo and transaction history are separate data. An unavailable quote or delayed provider response does not by itself establish that an asset balance is zero.

## Steps

1. Open the coin or token from Wallet or Search.
2. Read the available price and the displayed update time. The price card does not show provider names, Powered by labels or Saved price labels.
3. If a 24h chart control is visible, tap it to expand or collapse the available chart.
4. If there is no chart control, Oath has no usable chart data for that asset at present. You can still read an available quote.
5. Pull down on the asset screen to refresh, then check the timestamp again.

Quotes and charts depend on provider coverage. They may use cached values and do not guarantee an executable trade price. A transaction’s local-currency value can use today’s quote rather than the historical execution price.

# Why does my address need funds to activate?

Understand account activation, minimum balances and storage on Stellar, XRP Ledger, Solana, TRON, NEAR and Gram (TON). Oath does not charge an activation fee.

## Why a new address can need funding

Creating or importing a wallet gives you an address before that address necessarily exists as an account on the blockchain. Some networks require a reserve, some require funds for storage, and some deploy a wallet contract. These rules help limit spam and pay for maintaining or processing on-chain data. They are network rules, not an Oath subscription.

Oath does not charge or collect an activation fee. Fund the receiving address in your own wallet, not an address supplied by someone claiming to activate it for you. Network transaction fees, network account-creation charges, storage costs and an exchange’s withdrawal fees can still apply. Oath cannot waive these charges or change a network’s reserve.

A reserve or storage deposit is different from a fee: it may stay in an account while being unavailable to spend. A network fee is consumed under that network’s rules. Do not assume that every amount called activation is refundable.

## Stellar (XLM): a minimum account balance

An ordinary new Stellar account needs two base reserves. At the time of this update, one base reserve is 0.5 XLM, so a basic account needs 1 XLM. Oath reads the current ledger reserve for its notice. The sender must use a transfer flow that creates a new Stellar account; an ordinary payment to a nonexistent account is not enough.

The reserve remains in your Stellar account; Oath does not receive it. It normally cannot be spent while the account requires it. Trustlines and other ledger entries can increase the minimum, commonly by another base reserve each. For example, holding an issued token can require a trustline in addition to activation. Sponsored reserves can change who supplies the balance. Keep extra XLM available for transaction fees; sending an issued token alone does not create an ordinary new account.

Source: https://developers.stellar.org/docs/learn/fundamentals/lumens

## XRP Ledger (XRP): the base reserve

A new XRP Ledger address becomes an account when it receives enough XRP to meet the base reserve. The published Mainnet base reserve is currently 1 XRP; Oath uses the validated ledger’s current value. Additional owned objects can raise the reserve, currently generally 0.2 XRP per item, with exceptions and sponsorship rules.

Reserved XRP stays in the account and is normally unavailable for ordinary payments. It is not paid to Oath. Network transaction costs are separate and can consume XRP even below the reserve. Qualifying account deletion can recover part of a reserve, but has its own network rules and cost; removing a wallet from Oath does not delete its on-chain account. Activate with XRP first, not an issued token. An already existing account can receive smaller XRP payments.

Source: https://xrpl.org/docs/concepts/accounts/reserves

## Solana (SOL): account funding and token-account deposits

Solana accounts need enough SOL for their rent-exempt balance, which depends on the space they use. For an address that does not yet have a native account, Oath asks the network for the current minimum for a basic account rather than assuming every account needs the same amount. The SOL remains in that account; it is not an Oath activation payment. Keep additional SOL for future transaction fees.

USDC, USDT and other Solana tokens live in separate token accounts. A sender can create the required token account and fund its deposit while transferring a token, even if the wallet owner has no SOL balance. Receiving tokens therefore does not prove the owner’s native SOL account is funded. A token-account deposit is separate from the transaction fee; eligible token accounts can be closed to reclaim their remaining SOL under the token program’s rules. Account size and token extensions can change the deposit.

Source: https://solana.com/docs/core/accounts/account-structure

Source: https://solana.com/docs/tokens/basics/create-token-account

Source: https://solana.com/docs/tokens/basics/close-account

## TRON (TRX): account creation paid by the sender

A newly generated TRON address is activated by receiving TRX or a TRC-10 transfer from an existing account, or by an account-creation operation. Receiving only a TRC-20 token such as USDT does not perform that native-account activation.

For standard activation, the sender pays the network account-creation charge: currently 1 TRX, plus a possible 0.1 TRX creation Bandwidth charge when staked or delegated Bandwidth is insufficient. Parameters can change. Contract-based activation follows different Energy and Bandwidth rules. These are consumed network charges, not a minimum TRX balance held by the recipient and not an Oath fee. The amount sent to the recipient remains theirs. After activation, TRX or sufficient network resources are still needed to send, especially for TRC-20 tokens. A token transfer’s cost is not fixed by this activation example.

Source: https://developers.tron.network/docs/account

## NEAR: creating an implicit account and covering storage

Oath’s generated NEAR address is a 64-character implicit account ID. A native NEAR transfer creates that account on chain and credits the transferred balance. The warning applies to this implicit-address flow; it is not a way to register an arbitrary missing name ending in .near.

Keep enough NEAR for the account’s storage requirements and later transaction fees. Storage usage, account configuration and token-contract registration can affect the required amount, so this guide does not promise one universal activation deposit. NEAR reserved for storage is unavailable for other uses while that storage is required. Token registration can require a separate storage deposit with a token contract, and sending a token does not substitute for creating the native account. Oath does not collect these balances. Any storage refund depends on the account or contract’s supported rules; deleting the wallet in the app does not refund on-chain storage.

Source: https://github.com/near/nearcore/blob/master/docs/DataStructures/Account.md

Source: https://docs.near.org/protocol/storage/storage-staking

## Gram (TON): fund, then deploy the wallet contract

Oath displays this network as Gram and its native coin as GRAM. TON wallets are smart contracts. A new address can first receive funds while its contract is still uninitialized. The initial native-coin transfer should be non-bounceable; use the receiving address supplied by Oath and a sender that supports this network.

Funding the address and deploying the contract are different steps. Oath includes the wallet’s deployment data with its first outgoing transaction when required. Until the contract is active, the notice can remain even when the balance is positive. You do not need to repeatedly deposit just because deployment is still pending.

There is no single fixed deposit that guarantees every deployment or transfer. Keep enough native coin for the estimated deployment, transaction and storage costs. The unused balance remains in your account; actual network charges are consumed. Jettons such as USDT do not replace native coin for these costs. Oath does not take an activation fee.

Source: https://docs.ton.org/foundations/status

Source: https://docs.ton.org/foundations/fees

## What about the other supported networks?

Oath does not show this account-activation notice for ordinary wallet receipts on Bitcoin-family networks, EVM networks, Sui, Aptos or THORChain. This does not mean transactions are free. Sender fees, minimum transfer or dust rules, token-specific requirements and funds needed for a later outgoing transaction are different questions.

## Why the notice appears, disappears or stays visible

Oath checks the selected receiving address in the background. It shows this notice only when the network check confirms an absent or undeployed account. It does not block copying or sharing the address. An account already reported active does not get this activation notice, even if it later needs more funds for fees or other reserves.

A failed or unavailable network check is not proof that an account is inactive, so Oath does not show an activation warning for an unknown result. The absence of this notice is therefore not a guarantee that a transfer will succeed. Check the correct network, address, amount and sender review. Each address and network has its own state; activating one does not activate all your wallets.

## Steps

1. Choose the wallet you want to receive into, open Receive and select the correct asset and network.
2. If an activation notice appears below the address, read its network and amount. It concerns this address on this network, not every wallet in Oath.
3. Use the address shown in Receive to fund your own account on that same network. Follow the relevant network section below; sending a token may not activate the native account.
4. Check the sender’s review before confirming. Allow for any sender fee or exchange withdrawal fee so the amount actually received meets the requirement.
5. After the transfer confirms, reopen Receive to check again. On Gram (TON), funding and deploying the wallet contract are separate steps, so funding alone can leave a deployment notice.

Network values can change. Use the current amount shown in Oath and review the sender’s charges. Never share recovery words, a passphrase or a private key to activate an account. Oath does not charge an activation fee; network costs and third-party withdrawal fees may still apply.

## Related

- [Receive crypto with a QR code](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/receive-crypto.md): Share the receiving address for the wallet and network you intend to use.
- [What does “and more” mean on Receive?](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/receive-network-tokens.md): The example logos illustrate tokens on a network; they are not a limit on what its address can receive.

# Receive crypto with a QR code

Share the receiving address for the wallet and network you intend to use.

The QR is generated by the native iOS QR pipeline. The central asset mark is visual identification; always read the network and address as well.

The assets row or About this address explains what the selected network can receive. Examples do not mean every token on every other chain can be deposited here.

Receive does not require signing a transaction. It does not set a requested amount or add a card to Apple Wallet. You can share the public address without sharing recovery words or a private key.

## Steps

1. Choose the correct active wallet, then tap Receive on Home and select an asset. Receive on an asset screen opens that asset directly.
2. Check the sheet title, such as Receive Ethereum, and the network guidance directly beneath the QR code.
3. If an address-type or derivation selector appears in the top toolbar, choose the intended account format before sharing.
4. Read the full address near the bottom above Copy address and Share. Compare it with the wallet and network you intend to fund.
5. Let the sender scan the QR, or copy/share the public address. The QR encodes the address; the sender must also choose the correct network and asset.
6. After the sender broadcasts, refresh Home and check History. Use the transaction’s explorer record if confirmation or indexing is still pending.

The same-looking address can exist on multiple networks. The network must match, and the QR is an address, not a guarantee that the sender chose the correct chain.

# Copy or share your receiving address

Use Oath’s receive actions instead of retyping a long address.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

Copy address supplies the full value even if another screen abbreviates it. After pasting, compare the beginning, end and complete destination with the original before the sender confirms.

The share sheet sends only after you choose a destination and finish that app’s action. Canceling it does not create a payment request or transfer.

## Steps

1. Open Receive for the intended wallet and asset.
2. If necessary, choose the address type or Solana path from the top toolbar first.
3. Tap Copy address to copy the full address, or Share to open the native share sheet.
4. Tell the sender the exact network alongside the address. Sharing an address does not bridge between networks.
5. Ask the sender to compare the full address and complete a small test payment when appropriate before a larger transfer.

Only share a public receiving address or receiving QR. A private key, recovery phrase or recovery QR gives access to funds.

# What does “and more” mean on Receive?

The example logos illustrate tokens on a network; they are not a limit on what its address can receive.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

A token on Ethereum and the similarly named token on another chain have separate balances. Match the actual deployment and network at the sending service.

The list is explanatory rather than an exhaustive worldwide token registry. An unknown asset can require manual discovery, and unsupported standards may not offer a send flow.

## Steps

1. Open Receive for the intended network and read the sentence below the QR.
2. Tap the supported-assets row or About this address.
3. Read the network-specific explanation and compare the token’s actual contract or mint with the one you intend to receive.
4. Return to the QR and copy/share the address for that same network.
5. After a transfer, use asset search to add a supported token by its exact identity if discovery has not listed it.

Token discovery depends on the network, provider coverage and filtering. A received token may need an address lookup to appear, and receiving it does not guarantee a price. Never send a token on a different network just because its logo is shown.

# Choose a Bitcoin address type

Select the receiving format compatible with the service sending you BTC.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

Taproot, Native SegWit, wrapped SegWit and Legacy use different address formats and derivations within a compatible Bitcoin wallet. Selecting a type does not convert coins into another network.

An imported single key or account-scoped extended key can support fewer choices. Use the choices actually offered for that wallet; do not assume a full recovery-phrase account was restored.

When comparing an older receipt, retain its original address and transaction ID. New receive addresses can differ while still belonging to the same supported wallet.

## Steps

1. Open Bitcoin from Home and tap Receive.
2. Tap the address-type control.
3. Choose Taproot (BIP86), Native SegWit (BIP84), SegWit (BIP49), or Legacy (BIP44), where your imported material supports it.
4. Copy the newly displayed address or use its QR. Check the sender supports that format.

The choice affects receiving. The Bitcoin balance scan covers supported imported branches, not only the currently visible type. Uncompressed private keys support Legacy only; scoped extended keys cannot recover unrelated branches.

# Why can a Bitcoin receiving address change?

HD wallets derive multiple addresses rather than reusing one address forever.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

Address discovery scans a bounded sequence of unused HD addresses. Large runs of intentionally unused addresses can place later activity outside ordinary discovery.

Keep records of any unusual account index or derivation choices used in the original wallet. A single imported key cannot reproduce a full HD address tree.

Do not repeatedly generate and discard addresses as a test of recovery. Compare known public addresses and use the supported receive selection.

## Steps

1. Use the address currently shown in Receive for a new payment.
2. Keep the same wallet selected when checking past receipts.
3. Refresh to scan the supported address branches for history and balances.
4. If recovering a wallet with many intentionally skipped unused addresses, tell support about that pattern without sending secrets.

The scanner uses a gap of 20 unused addresses per supported branch. Addresses far beyond an unused gap may not be discovered. Previously derived addresses still belong to the same wallet.

# Choose Phantom or Trust Wallet’s Solana path

Match the Solana account derived by the wallet you are recovering.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

Phantom and Trust Wallet conventions derive different accounts from the same recovery phrase. Selecting the path changes which Solana address the receive screen shows and which account its data follows.

Before changing a path, finish any pending send or dApp review. Return to the dApp and reconnect or choose the matching account if it expects a different address.

A single imported Solana key can only expose its original account; it does not gain both derivations by selecting a menu option.

## Steps

1. Open Solana’s asset screen and tap Receive.
2. Tap the address-path control if it is available.
3. Select Phantom or Trust Wallet. Phantom is the default for phrase-based wallets.
4. Check the new address and QR, then return to the asset screen to view data for that active address.

The paths derive different accounts from the same phrase. Changing paths does not transfer funds between accounts. A directly imported private key has its original address and does not offer two HD paths.

# Check the network before a transfer

Prevent address and network mismatches before the sender broadcasts.

Public addresses can share a format across different networks. That does not make the chains interchangeable or prove a deposit service can recover the transfer.

If already sent, retain the transaction ID and contact the receiving service using official channels. Do not pay an unsolicited recovery service or disclose keys.

Receiving shares a public destination; it does not sign a transfer. The sender must select the same network and asset deployment as the address you are showing.

## Steps

1. Compare the network named in Oath with the network selected by the sender or exchange.
2. For tokens, confirm that the contract or mint belongs to that same network.
3. If the sender asks for a memo or tag, verify its requirements for the actual destination instead of inventing one.
4. If a transfer already used the wrong network, keep the transaction ID and contact support with public details only.

A matching symbol or 0x address does not mean funds will appear on the network you expected. Recovery is not guaranteed, and another transfer does not reverse the first one.

# Read your transaction activity

See the direction, time and amount for an asset’s transactions.

The logo is the asset identity; the badge describes the activity. Neither an attractive logo nor a familiar ticker guarantees that a token is trustworthy.

Local-currency amounts can use current available prices and exchange rates. They are not a historical receipt of the original exchange rate. Amounts respect your hidden-balance setting.

Spam filtering applies to activity lists, searches and asset previews. Provider coverage can also limit the records available to Oath.

## Steps

1. Open History for the active wallet’s available activity, or scroll to Activity on a particular asset.
2. Read the action and asset symbol together, such as Sent USDT or Received USDC. Failed, Canceled and Replaced identify a different outcome when evidence is available.
3. Use the coin or token logo to identify the asset. Its small overlaid badge indicates the direction or outcome.
4. Read the time beneath the action label. Date headings group entries; the local-currency value is on the opposite side with the native quantity underneath.
5. Tap an entry for status, network, available fee information, addresses and the transaction ID.

Some providers supply incomplete history or do not identify every transfer. Local-currency amounts may use current available prices, not the price at the time of the transaction.

# Open transaction details

Review the useful details without navigating raw blockchain data.

The header uses the coin or token logo with an action or status badge. Read the text status as well; an icon alone is not sufficient to establish confirmation.

The fee is a network cost, separate from the transferred quantity. A failed on-chain transaction can still consume fees. Missing information remains unavailable rather than being invented.

Explorer and share-link actions use the transaction’s network. A receipt image is convenient to share, but a recipient should verify the public transaction and its outcome.

## Steps

1. Open History or an asset’s Activity and tap a transaction.
2. Read the asset logo and action/status badge, then compare the asset quantity with the local-currency estimate.
3. Check Status, Time, Network and the available Network fee. Pending, failed, canceled and replaced entries do not all mean a successful transfer.
4. Use the copy buttons for full addresses and the transaction ID. Shortened text on the screen is only a display abbreviation.
5. Tap the ellipsis in the top toolbar for Share Screenshot, Share Link or View on Explorer.

Missing provider fields are not fabricated. A displayed local-currency fee is a conversion and can differ from the value at the transaction’s original time.

# Understand pending, confirmed and failed activity

Use status to distinguish a submitted transaction from a settled one.

Open the exact transaction and compare its network and full identifier. A pending status, a signed request and a confirmed transfer represent different stages.

The app distinguishes sending/submission progress from a confirmed network result. An outgoing request can be signed before the network has accepted it.

A failed execution can consume network fees without delivering the intended assets. A locally rejected request before signing is a different outcome.

If the network result is uncertain, preserve the transaction ID and wait for a definitive status before making a duplicate payment.

## Steps

1. Open the transaction from History or its asset’s Activity.
2. Read the status text alongside the header badge. Pending means the final outcome is not yet established.
3. For a confirmed transaction, check the actual transfer or contract result in details and the explorer.
4. For failed, canceled or replaced activity, inspect the related transaction and fees before deciding whether to try again.
5. If the provider is delayed, refresh and inspect the same transaction ID; do not assume a missing update means a transfer failed.

A failed transaction may still incur a network fee on some chains. A pending incoming payment is not final; provider lag or a chain reorganization can change the result.

# What do Canceled and Replaced mean?

These labels are shown only when the app has evidence of the corresponding transaction state.

Open the exact transaction and compare its network and full identifier. A pending status, a signed request and a confirmed transfer represent different stages.

Replacement can cause the original transaction and its successor to have different outcomes. Inspect the relevant identifiers and final network result before counting a payment twice.

A cancellation attempt is itself subject to network ordering and fees where supported. A confirmed original transfer cannot be undone by deleting its history entry or disconnecting a dApp.

## Steps

1. Open the affected activity row and read its status.
2. If a replacement transaction ID is shown, copy it or check the relevant explorer.
3. Compare the final confirmed transaction instead of counting both entries as separate transfers.
4. Refresh when a replacement is still pending.

Oath does not infer cancellation merely because a request failed or a transaction disappeared from one response. Support varies by chain and provider. This build does not offer a user action to cancel or replace a transfer.

# Read the network fee

See a transaction’s available fee converted to your chosen currency.

The fee pays for network execution or inclusion and is separate from the amount transferred. Token sends commonly need a native fee asset as well as the token.

A failed on-chain transaction may still consume fees. An estimated local-currency fee can vary with the market price and is not an exact historical fiat receipt.

Open the exact transaction and compare its network and full identifier. A pending status, a signed request and a confirmed transfer represent different stages.

## Steps

2. Find Network fee when the provider supplied it.
3. Change the display currency in Settings → Currency if needed.
4. Use View on Explorer to inspect the network’s original fee information.

The fee is separate from a token’s transfer amount. The local value uses an available conversion rate; unavailable fee information is not treated as a verified zero.

# Copy a transaction ID or address

Use the small copy controls beside shortened identifiers.

The middle ellipsis is only a display abbreviation. Copy preserves the entire address or transaction ID; comparing just the first and last characters is not enough to establish a match.

An address identifies an account or destination. A transaction ID identifies a particular public transaction; use the identifier requested by the person helping you.

Open the exact transaction and compare its network and full identifier. A pending status, a signed request and a confirmed transfer represent different stages.

Copying returns the complete transaction identifier even when the visible row is abbreviated. Paste it into the explorer for that same network, not a different chain with a similar format.

A transaction ID is public, but sharing it can reveal associated account activity. It is useful for support and payment verification; recovery words are not needed.

## Steps

1. Open the transaction.
2. Find the address or transaction ID row. Long values are shortened in the middle for readability.
3. Tap the copy icon next to the value.
4. Paste it into the appropriate network explorer or your support message.

The copied value is complete even when the on-screen label is shortened. A transaction ID is public; recovery material is not.

# View a transaction on its explorer

Open the public network record inside Oath’s native browser.

Open the exact transaction and compare its network and full identifier. A pending status, a signed request and a confirmed transfer represent different stages.

Check the explorer hostname and network before reading the result. Some transactions contain several transfers, approvals or contract events, so the first displayed amount may not describe the whole operation.

An explorer is external content. Close it to return to Oath and avoid any advertising or links requesting recovery material.

## Steps

4. Read confirmation status and the actual transfers or events. A transaction may contain several actions.
5. Close the browser to return to Oath. Share Link in the same menu shares the public record without opening it first.

The explorer is an independent website. It never needs your recovery phrase or private key to display a transaction.

# Send coins and tokens

Choose the right wallet, network, recipient and amount, then review and authorize a transfer.

Sending is available for supported assets on Bitcoin-family networks, EVM networks, TRON, Solana, Gram, Aptos, Sui, NEAR, XRP Ledger, Stellar and THORChain. The selected asset’s flow determines what is supported; a discoverable token is not a guarantee that every unusual token standard can be sent.

The displayed local-currency amount is an estimate. The quantity in asset units is what the transfer spends. Fee estimates and spendable balances may change during review, so Oath can require you to review again.

Insufficient gas, an invalid recipient, a locked wallet or a failed network check can prevent submission. Correct the specific issue and review again. Never treat an error as proof that an earlier uncertain submission cannot have reached the network.

## Steps

1. Check the active wallet on Home. Tap Send and choose the exact coin or token; the same ticker can exist on different networks.
2. Paste or scan the recipient address, or choose a saved contact. Compare the complete address and network with the recipient’s instructions.
3. Enter a destination tag or memo when the recipient requires one. Continue only after any address or memo validation is resolved.
4. Enter the amount in asset units, or switch to local currency when a usable price is available. Max leaves room for the applicable fees and reserves.
5. Continue to review. Check the wallet, network, asset, recipient, amount and maximum network fee. Read any activation, reserve or token-registration guidance.
6. Confirm and authenticate when requested. Keep the result open until Oath reports a submission or an error; a review screen alone does not send funds.
7. Open the resulting transaction in History. Use its status and explorer record to distinguish pending from confirmed. If a response is uncertain, check the existing transaction before trying another transfer.

A direct send stays on the selected network. It does not swap assets or bridge funds to another chain.

# Review wallet permissions and connected apps

Inspect token allowances, NFT access, connected apps and supported account-control permissions for the selected wallet.

EVM standard allowances and NFT approvals, TRON TRC-20 approvals and Solana SPL/Token-2022 delegates have different removal instructions. Oath prepares the supported action for each permission rather than treating every chain alike.

An asset name or logo helps you recognize a row, but it is not evidence that the contract is safe. Compare the full network and addresses. Some contracts have no reliable name and remain identified by their address.

Unknown off-chain signatures, custom contracts and some account-level privileges cannot be comprehensively discovered. A blank list is not a certificate that the wallet has no permissions.

## Steps

1. Open Settings → Permissions and check the wallet shown at the top. Select a different wallet there if needed.
2. Wait for the scan to finish, then open Token access, Collectible access or Account control to see the permissions found for that wallet.
3. Read the network group and exact asset or contract on each row. Open a row to inspect the approved address and scope of its access.
4. Open Connected DApps to manage WalletConnect sessions. Disconnecting a session and revoking on-chain access are separate actions.
5. Use the filter menu’s Select action for multiple removals, or swipe a removable row. Review the revocation and fees before confirming.
6. After submission, check Recent changes and refresh the scan. Read Scan coverage for partial, unavailable or unindexed networks.

Revocations are network transactions and require fees. Removing a token from view, deleting a local wallet or disconnecting a dApp does not revoke its on-chain allowance.

# Report a bug

Give enough detail for the problem to be reproduced without exposing secrets.

Return to the relevant screen to confirm the setting or saved entry. Canceling an edit should not be treated as an applied change.

Include the app version, device/iOS version, screen, exact steps and nonsecret error text. For a transaction issue, add its network and public transaction ID if one exists.

A screenshot can help, but review it first for balances, names and other private information. Never attach recovery phrases, keys, passwords, pairing URIs or raw signed payloads.

If a submission is pending or uncertain, check its existing transaction before attempting another transfer while waiting for support.

## Steps

1. Tap Submit a Bug to open the GitHub issue tracker.
2. Describe what you expected, what happened and the shortest sequence of steps that reproduces it.
3. Include the app version, iOS version and affected network when relevant.
4. Attach a screenshot only after checking it for private information.

Do not share recovery phrases, private keys or backup passwords. For a sensitive report, use Contact Us instead of a public issue.

# Contact Oath support

# Use Bitcoin Cash in Oath

Receive, send and inspect Bitcoin Cash assets using the correct account and network.

Use the Bitcoin Cash address and supported format. A Bitcoin transaction and a Bitcoin Cash transaction are separate; a familiar-looking address is not enough to select a network.

Discovery, activity and price coverage can differ between native assets and tokens. If a quote is unavailable, the token quantity can still be correct; do not interpret missing market data as a zero price.

Check the active wallet before every action. Imported private keys may expose fewer accounts or address types than a full recovery-phrase wallet.

## Steps

1. Open Wallet → Search and find Bitcoin Cash or BCH. Select the intended native asset or token.
2. Read the quantity, available price and Activity. Use Asset Information to verify a token’s full identity.
3. Tap Receive, check the network notice and copy the complete public address. Confirm the sending service supports this exact network.
4. For an outgoing transfer, tap Send, enter the recipient and any required memo or tag, then choose an amount.
5. Review the fee and any account requirements before confirming. Complete authentication when requested.
6. Check the transaction’s status and use the ellipsis → View on Explorer to verify its public outcome.

Uses Bitcoin Cash addresses and its own history. Do not send Bitcoin (BTC) to this network.

## Related

- [Search for a coin or token](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/search-assets.md): Find an asset by its name, symbol, network or saved token address.

- [Open an asset’s screen](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/asset-screen.md): View one asset’s value, quantity, market information and activity.

# Use Ethereum and EVM networks

One wallet can show the same public address across EVM networks while tracking each network separately.

The current EVM catalog includes Ethereum, Arbitrum, Arc, Avalanche C-Chain, Base, BNB Smart Chain, Fantom, Flare, Gnosis, HyperEVM, Linea, Monad, Optimism, Polygon, Robinhood Chain, Scroll, Somnia, Story, Taiko, Telos EVM, Unichain and X Layer.

A contract address is meaningful together with its network. Even when two chains use the same 0x account address, their coins, tokens, approvals and transaction histories remain separate.

Direct sends stay on the selected network. A dApp swap or bridge can involve separate approvals and transactions; review each request and never infer a destination chain from the token ticker alone.

## Steps

1. Select Wallet, then Search, and look for the intended network or select it through Receive.
2. Check the network name before sharing its address.
3. View tokens on that network or search by an exact token contract address.
4. Open transactions from the relevant asset’s Activity; their explorer links are network-specific.

Keep the network’s fee asset available for token transfers. Arc is a special case with native USDC; follow its own fee review.

# Understand USDC on Arc

Arc uses USDC as its native asset in the app’s network integration.

Quantity, market price, logo and transaction history are separate data. An unavailable quote or delayed provider response does not by itself establish that an asset balance is zero.

Native USDC on Arc is the network’s base asset in this integration. An ERC-20 USDC deployment on Ethereum, Base or another network is not interchangeable with that Arc balance.

When sending, review the fee units and exact network rather than assuming ETH always pays gas on an EVM-compatible chain.

Discovery of other Arc tokens and their quotes depends on supported provider coverage. An incomplete index must not be interpreted as proof that no tokens exist.

## Steps

1. Select Wallet, then Search, and look for Arc or USDC and select the Arc entry.
2. Check that the network is Arc before using Receive.
3. Review its native USDC balance and activity on the asset screen.
4. For other Arc tokens, search the exact contract address and verify the selected network before adding.

An Ethereum or another network’s USDC balance is separate. Mainnet and testnet are distinct; use the network identity shown by the app and the sender.

# Scan a token address from Home

Use the viewfinder button to bring QR text into asset search without typing it.

The Home scanner fills asset search. It does not send a payment, approve a contract, connect a dApp or automatically open a scanned website.

Not every QR contains a token address. A receiving address, payment URI or unrelated text may produce no token result; copying a project’s exact token contract or mint address can help.

To import a recovery phrase, use the dedicated scan action inside Import wallet. Keep private recovery material out of Home search and support messages.

## Steps

1. Return to Home with the Wallet icon and tap the viewfinder in the top bar.
2. Allow camera access when iOS asks, then point the camera at a public token-address QR you trust.
3. After a code is read, the scanner closes and Oath opens asset Search with the scanned text.
4. If the text identifies a supported token, review the result’s network and full contract or mint address before adding it.
5. If scanning cannot start, check Camera permission in iOS Settings or paste the address into Wallet → Search.

Scanning is an input shortcut, not a trust check. Confirm the network and complete address using an independent source.

# Open the current wallet’s settings from Home

Reach the active wallet’s management screen using the toolbar shortcut that appears after scrolling.

The symbol uses the actual wallet color. Its center is the main color and its surrounding border uses the system’s lighter hierarchical rendering.

The two appearances have different destinations: sliders opens app Settings, while the colored wallet symbol opens current-wallet settings. To reach Currency, Language or Appearance, return to the top of Home and use sliders.

The shortcut does not switch wallets. Recovery and private-key actions still use their own authentication and warning steps.

## Steps

1. Open Home using the Wallet icon in the bottom navigation.
2. At the top of Home, the top-right sliders icon opens the main app Settings.
3. Scroll down through Assets. As the header scrolls away, the sliders icon changes to the current wallet’s colored square symbol.
4. Tap that colored icon to open the current wallet’s settings in a slide-up presentation.
5. Choose an available action, such as customization, iCloud backup or viewing recovery information. Close the screen when finished.

The controls can be mirrored for right-to-left languages. Identify them by their symbols or VoiceOver names rather than relying only on left or right placement.

# Read wallet balances and the active-wallet badge

Recognize each wallet by its color and check its available value beside the disclosure arrow.

The icon has no separate colored tile behind it. It uses the wallet’s selected color, so changing Customize Wallet also changes its visual identity in the list.

Values are based on the balances, prices and exchange rates available to Oath. An inactive wallet can have older cached information; a listed value is not proof of a fresh network check.

Large accessibility text can move the amount below the name to preserve readability. The value still belongs to the same wallet row.

In the Home switcher, tapping a wallet selects it. In Settings → Wallets, tapping a row opens management instead. Both lists share the same wallet icon, balance and active badge.

## Steps

1. Tap the wallet-name capsule above Home’s balance to open the switcher. To manage wallets instead, open Settings with the sliders icon, then choose Wallets.
2. Find a wallet by its name and colored square symbol. Passphrase wallets can also show a descriptive subtitle.
3. Read each row’s available local-currency value. This is that wallet’s saved valuation, not the combined value of every wallet.
4. Look for a small check badge on the icon to identify the active wallet. The check is no longer placed beside the amount.
5. If values appear as dots, return Home and tap the total balance to reveal them. Use Settings → Currency to choose another display currency.

The active-wallet badge identifies the wallet used by Home and History. Use the Home name capsule to switch; opening a management row in Settings does not by itself change the active wallet.

# View the active wallet’s full transaction history

Review available coin and token activity together across the active wallet’s networks.

This view combines available activity for the active wallet. It does not merge unrelated wallets, and Solana activity follows the currently selected Solana address path.

A history row represents an asset’s activity within a transaction. One blockchain transaction can therefore produce more than one row when multiple assets are involved.

“Full history” means the available records for this wallet, after safety filtering. Provider limits, incomplete synchronization and unsupported historical details can leave gaps.

## Steps

1. Tap the history icon, shown as a clock with a circular arrow, in the bottom navigation.
2. Review the most recent available entries, grouped by date. Each row identifies the action and asset, its time, and available amounts.
3. Scroll for older entries and use the additional-activity control when it is shown to load more saved history.
4. Tap an entry to open its transaction details, or use the filter icon in the top bar to narrow the list.
5. To look for a particular transaction, select History and then the separate Search icon. Return to Wallet when you want the portfolio view.

If an expected entry is absent, clear search and filters, refresh Home or the asset, and compare the exact public account on its network explorer.

# Search transactions by ID, address or amount

Find a transaction using information you already know, within the active wallet’s available history.

Search works across available stored history before the visible page limit. An address can match supplied sender or recipient information even if the list shows only one representative counterparty.

Amount searches use available prices and the selected display currency. A local-currency match may change with the quote; a transaction ID is a more stable way to identify a transfer.

History filters remain in effect during history search. Searching does not bypass spam filtering or fetch records a provider has never supplied.

## Steps

1. Tap History first, then the separate magnifying-glass Search icon.
2. Confirm the field says Search transactions. Enter a transaction ID, sender or recipient address, asset name, symbol, or network.
3. You can also search an amount in native units or an available displayed local-currency amount. Add a currency code or symbol when it helps distinguish a fiat value.
4. Open a result to compare its full transaction ID, network, addresses and status.
5. If a result is missing, clear the query and any active filters, then try the exact transaction ID or address. To search assets again, select Wallet before Search.

A short address fragment or common amount can match several entries. Compare the complete transaction ID before treating a result as the transfer you intended.

# Filter transaction history

Narrow activity by network, asset, direction, status, date and quantity without changing the underlying records.

Selections within one category are alternatives; categories combine. For example, Received plus USDC plus a date range means incoming USDC entries in that range.

Amount limits are measured in the asset’s native units, not local currency. A minimum of 10 means 10 tokens or coins. Select one asset first when you need a meaningful quantity comparison.

Today uses the current calendar day. The seven-day and thirty-day periods include today; custom dates include both selected days. Entries without a usable timestamp may not match a date filter.

The number on the filter button counts active filter categories, not individual selected networks or assets. In one asset’s View All screen, the asset and account scope is fixed, so broader network and asset selectors are omitted.

## Steps

1. Open History and tap the filter icon in the top bar. The sheet starts with your current selections.
2. Choose one or more Networks and Assets when those choices are available. Asset choices refer to an exact asset on its network, not just a shared ticker.
3. Choose transaction types such as Sent, Received or self-transfers, and any statuses you want to include.
4. Select a date period or custom start and end dates. Optionally enter a minimum, maximum or both under Amount.
5. Tap the native checkmark to apply the choices. Cancel or dismiss the sheet to leave the current results unchanged.
6. Use the active filter chips above the results to remove individual categories, or choose Reset Filters to clear them. If resetting inside the sheet, tap the checkmark to apply that reset.

A disabled checkmark means a range needs correction, such as a minimum above its maximum or a start date after its end. No matching results can simply mean the combined filters are too narrow.

# View all transactions for one coin or token

Move from an asset’s five-entry preview to a dedicated history for that exact asset and account.

View All stays limited to the selected token or coin, its account and its network. Opening USDT on one network does not include another network’s USDT or every token on that chain.

If there are five or fewer visible entries, there is no View All button because the preview already contains all currently available entries.

The threshold is based on visible history after safety filtering. Hidden spam and unavailable provider records do not force the button to appear.

## Steps

1. Open the coin or token from Wallet or Search and scroll to Activity.
2. The preview shows up to five latest visible entries. Each row names the action and asset and shows its time and available amounts.
3. When more than five visible entries are available, tap View All at the end of the preview.
4. Browse older entries on the new screen. Search there or use its filter icon to narrow the same asset’s history.
5. Tap a transaction for details, or go back to the asset screen. Use the bottom History view separately for activity across the wallet.

An absent View All button is not proof that no other on-chain activity ever occurred. Check the correct account and explorer if a known transaction is missing.

# How Oath hides spam and phishing activity

Understand why suspicious or unverified token entries can be absent from your activity lists.

The same visibility rules apply to the full history, asset previews, transaction search, filter choices and transaction details. Previously saved activity is also checked, so old spam does not need a fresh arrival to be hidden.

Oath combines available provider verification with network-specific asset catalogs and local checks. A token is matched by its network and exact contract, mint, issuer or asset reference. Matching a popular symbol or having a quoted price is not enough.

Unlisted tokens are hidden by default from history unless you have explicitly chosen to track them. Explicit tracking does not override detected phishing metadata, known blocked-token evidence or zero-value transfer rules.

Filtering changes the app’s presentation. It does not delete public blockchain records, reverse a transfer or revoke a contract allowance. The explorer can still show entries that Oath hides.

## Steps

1. Use History or an asset’s Activity as usual. Safety filtering runs automatically; no separate switch is required.
2. If an unexpected token is absent, check whether it is unverified or has a suspicious name containing a link or a claim instruction.
3. For an expected legitimate transfer, verify the network, public account and full token contract or asset identity using independent information.
4. For supported manual-lookup networks, you can deliberately add a token you recognize through Wallet → Search. Review the full identity before adding it.
5. If a discrepancy remains, compare the public explorer record or contact support with the network and transaction ID.

No filter can recognize every scam, and an unlisted token is not automatically fraudulent. Never follow a claim link from unsolicited token metadata or use a lookalike address copied from unfamiliar activity.

## Related

- [Understand verified and manually added tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/unverified-tokens.md): Learn why automatic discovery can omit a token and what changes when you choose to track it.
- [Why can a transaction show zero?](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/zero-value-transactions.md): Distinguish a rounded fiat amount, a zero-value contract action and a hidden spam transfer.
- [Why isn’t a token appearing?](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/token-not-found.md): Check the wallet, network, address and lookup result before assuming funds are missing.

# Why can a transaction show zero?

Distinguish a rounded fiat amount, a zero-value contract action and a hidden spam transfer.

Zero-value incoming transfers and ordinary zero-value token-transfer entries are hidden by the history safety rules. Attackers can use such entries to put lookalike addresses into a wallet’s activity.

Oath can retain zero-value outgoing or self native-coin actions, and zero-value outgoing outcomes such as Failed, Canceled or Replaced. Hiding every zero would also hide meaningful actions.

A zero local-currency display, an unavailable quote and a zero native transfer are different situations. The detailed public transaction helps distinguish them.

## Steps

1. Compare the local-currency amount with the native quantity underneath it.
2. If the local value rounds to zero but the native quantity is nonzero, the transfer can simply be too small to display at that currency’s normal precision.
3. If the native amount is also zero, open the transaction and check its status, network fee and explorer record.
4. For an outgoing native-coin entry, consider whether it records a contract call or another action that transfers no native coin but still has a network fee.
5. If you do not recognize the activity, compare the complete sender, recipient and transaction ID. Do not rely on a short address fragment.

Filtering a zero-value entry is not the same as canceling it. On-chain records and any fees already paid are separate from the app’s activity display.

## Related

- [How Oath hides spam and phishing activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/spam-history.md): Understand why suspicious or unverified token entries can be absent from your activity lists.
- [Read the network fee](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/network-fee.md): See a transaction’s available fee converted to your chosen currency.
- [Understand pending, confirmed and failed activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/transaction-status.md): Use status to distinguish a submitted transaction from a settled one.

Applies to app version: Oath 4.1.14

# Understand verified and manually added tokens

Learn why automatic discovery can omit a token and what changes when you choose to track it.

Automatic token discovery uses available verification lists. A new or obscure legitimate token can be missing from a list, so “unverified” does not by itself mean “scam.”

Manually adding a supported token records your choice to track it. It does not verify its issuer, grant spending permission, buy the token, or guarantee a price and complete history.

History still hides identified phishing metadata, blocked tokens and protected zero-value transfers even when a token is tracked. An explorer may therefore show more raw activity than Oath.

## Steps

1. First confirm the active wallet and the network on which you expect the token.
2. If the token is absent, check its full contract, mint or asset reference using information you trust independently.
3. For supported EVM networks, TRON or Solana, select Wallet then Search and paste the exact token address.
4. Review every matching result’s network and token identity. Add only the intended token, then finish with the checkmark.
5. Return to the asset and review any available quantity, quote and activity. Refresh if a recent transfer has not appeared.

Never decide by symbol alone. Tokens with the same name on the same or different networks can have different contracts and issuers.

## Related

- [Find and add a token by address](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/add-custom-token.md): Look up a supported contract or mint address and review its details before adding it.
- [Why isn’t a token appearing?](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/token-not-found.md): Check the wallet, network, address and lookup result before assuming funds are missing.
- [How Oath hides spam and phishing activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/spam-history.md): Understand why suspicious or unverified token entries can be absent from your activity lists.

# Use the checkmark to finish an action

The native checkmark replaces text Done controls in supported screens and sheets.

The checkmark is an action control, and its meaning follows the screen you are on. It can finish editing, close a completed flow or apply a draft.

Cancel, Close, Back and destructive actions keep their own purposes. Do not use the checkmark as a substitute for reading a removal or permanent-deletion confirmation.

Native alerts, keyboards and browser controls are drawn by iOS and can use system-provided labels. Older supported iOS versions can also display a different native treatment.

## Steps

1. When you have finished reordering wallets, tap the checkmark in the top bar instead of looking for a text Done button.
2. After Add Token succeeds, use the checkmark confirmation to finish that sheet.
3. In history filters, choose your options and tap the checkmark to apply the complete selection.
4. If the confirmation is disabled, finish the operation or correct any invalid field before trying again.
5. With VoiceOver, listen for the action name, such as Done or Apply. The visual icon still has a localized accessibility label.

The small check badge on a wallet icon means that wallet is active. It is different from the tappable checkmark used to finish an action.

## Related

- [Reorder your wallets](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/reorder-wallets.md): Put frequently used wallets where you want them in the list.
- [Filter transaction history](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/filter-transactions.md): Narrow activity by network, asset, direction, status, date and quantity without changing the underlying records.
- [Find and add a token by address](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/add-custom-token.md): Look up a supported contract or mint address and review its details before adding it.

# Authenticate before opening Passcode & Face ID

Protect changes to app security with a separate authentication step.

Unlocking the app and entering its security settings are separate checks. Returning after the app locks can require authentication again.

If app passcode protection is disabled, there is no existing app passcode to enter. You can access the screen to set one, then confirm the new six-digit code.

When you finish enabling a new passcode, Oath attempts biometric setup when available. Turning on Face ID itself uses the biometric prompt rather than another current-passcode entry inside that enable flow.

## Steps

1. Open the main Settings screen from the sliders icon at the top of Home.
2. Tap Passcode & Face ID. If biometric protection is enabled, complete the biometric prompt.
3. If biometrics are disabled or the flow offers a passcode fallback, enter your current app passcode.
4. After authentication, review or change passcode protection, biometrics, Require Passcode timing or App Switcher Privacy.
5. If you cancel authentication, return to Settings and start again when ready.

Your app passcode is not your recovery phrase, BIP-39 passphrase or iCloud backup password. Security changes do not replace a separate recovery backup.

## Related

- [Enable passcode protection](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/enable-passcode.md): Require authentication to enter Oath.
- [Enable Face ID or Touch ID](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/enable-face-id.md): Use the device’s biometric authentication for faster access.
- [Choose when Oath locks](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/auto-lock.md): Control how long Oath stays unlocked after moving to the background.

# Open and search the Help Center

Find a feature’s instructions inside Oath and return to the app when you are finished.

Each guide describes one feature or question and identifies the app version it covers. Older release articles at articles.oathwallet.org can describe a different interface.

The Help Center is readable without importing a wallet or providing recovery material. Article screenshots use example wallets; do not send funds to example addresses.

Submit a Bug and Request a Feature open the project’s issue page. Contact Us opens an email draft to care@oathwallet.org; writing a draft does not send it automatically.

5. Close the in-app browser to return to Oath. Use Contact Us, Submit a Bug or Request a Feature from Settings if you need a different kind of help.

Never put a recovery phrase, private key, app passcode or backup password into a support form or message. Public transaction IDs are normally enough to start a transaction investigation.

# Use Max and understand spendable balance

See why the maximum you can send may be lower than the total displayed on Home.

Native-coin Max needs to leave enough for transaction costs. UTXO fees depend on inputs and transaction size; account-based networks may retain mandatory balances or reserves.

For a token, the entire token balance may be transferable while a different native asset pays gas. A token with no reliable quote can still be entered in asset units.

Fee estimates are network-specific and can change. A maximum fee is a spending limit or estimate used in that review, not a promise that the exact amount will be charged.

In 4.1.14, Max keeps the full calculated amount. Send and review values can show more digits than compact balance displays; signing still uses exact atomic units.

Fiat entry accepts at most two fractional digits. Send Max retains the full native amount used for signing; a rounded fiat display does not replace that amount. Tiny nonzero fiat values use a less-than bound instead of appearing as zero.

## Steps

1. Select the intended asset and enter the recipient first.
2. Tap Max on the amount page. Read the resulting quantity in asset units.
3. For token transfers, check that you also hold the network’s native fee asset.
4. Continue to review and read the network fee plus any activation, reserve or storage requirement.
5. If the available amount changes, return to amount and calculate Max again. Confirm only after reviewing the updated total.
6. Check History after submission; do not repeatedly send because a balance refresh is delayed.

A displayed portfolio total is a valuation, not a promise that all of it is spendable.

## Related

- [Send coins and tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/send-availability.md): Choose the right wallet, network, recipient and amount, then review and authorize a transfer.
- [Read the network fee](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/network-fee.md): See a transaction’s available fee converted to your chosen currency.

# Enter destination tags and memos

Include the extra reference an exchange or shared receiving account needs to credit your transfer.

An exchange may use one address for many customers and distinguish deposits with a tag or memo. A valid address alone can therefore be insufficient.

Text memos, numeric IDs and hashes are different formats. Use the field and type displayed for the selected chain; leading characters and case can matter.

Oath cannot assign a missing deposit to your exchange account after broadcast. Do not resend a second payment merely to fix a tag on the first.

## Steps

1. Open the recipient’s deposit instructions and confirm the asset and network.
2. In Oath, select that asset and paste the deposit address.
3. For XRP Ledger enter the requested destination tag. For Stellar select the required memo type before entering its exact value.
4. For other networks with a memo field, follow the recipient’s instructions exactly; do not invent a memo if none is required.
5. Review the address, memo/tag, amount and network together on the final screen.
6. After sending, retain the transaction ID. If an exchange does not credit it, contact that exchange with the public transaction details.

Memos and on-chain messages can become public. Never put a recovery phrase, private key, password or personal secret in them.

## Related

- [Send coins and tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/send-availability.md): Choose the right wallet, network, recipient and amount, then review and authorize a transfer.
- [Check the network before a transfer](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/wrong-network.md): Prevent address and network mismatches before the sender broadcasts.

# Set Bitcoin transfer options

Understand Replace by fee and the optional public on-chain message before sending.

The message is stored publicly with the transfer using OP_RETURN and contributes to transaction size and fees. A byte count is not necessarily the same as a character count.

Bitcoin node policies differ. Larger messages can be rejected by stricter nodes even when they fit the app’s supported limit.

RBF signals replacement policy; some Bitcoin nodes allow replacement even when that signal is off. The switch is not a guarantee that an unconfirmed transaction cannot be replaced.

## Steps

1. Choose Bitcoin, enter the recipient and continue to the amount page.
2. Open Transfer options from the amount page.
3. Enable Replace by fee only if you want the transaction to signal replacement eligibility. The option is off by default.
4. Optionally enter an on-chain message. Read the byte count and network-specific limit.
5. Confirm the options with the checkmark, then review the updated transaction and fee.
6. After broadcast, use the transaction’s status and explorer to follow it. Enabling RBF does not itself submit a replacement.

Never put secrets in an on-chain message. Confirmed blockchain content cannot be edited like a chat message.

## Related

- [Send coins and tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/send-availability.md): Choose the right wallet, network, recipient and amount, then review and authorize a transfer.
- [What do Canceled and Replaced mean?](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/canceled-replaced.md): These labels are shown only when the app has evidence of the corresponding transaction state.
- [Read the network fee](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/network-fee.md): See a transaction’s available fee converted to your chosen currency.

# Resolve a transfer that cannot be sent

Work out whether the problem is validation, fees, authorization, provider access or an uncertain submission.

A local validation error normally means a transfer has not been prepared. A lost response after broadcast is different: the network may already have the transaction.

Simulation and preflight failures can reflect insufficient funds, slippage, a changed allowance or contract conditions. Repeatedly confirming unchanged data does not fix those conditions.

Keep Oath available for status checks. Background work can pause when iOS suspends the app; reopening and unlocking lets pending work resume.

## Steps

1. Read the error and identify whether it occurred before authorization, during submission or while waiting for confirmation.
2. Check the selected wallet, recipient network, token identity and any required memo or tag.
3. Check the native fee balance and account activation, reserve or registration guidance. Reduce the amount if needed.
4. If authentication was canceled, return to the review and authenticate again. Never enter your recovery phrase into a dApp or support form.
5. If Oath has a transaction ID or reports a pending/uncertain submission, inspect that same transaction in History or its explorer before attempting another transfer.
6. If it is definitely failed or rejected, correct the reason and make a fresh review. Contact support with the network, public transaction ID and error text if needed.

Do not send recovery words, private keys, passcodes or raw signing payloads to support.

## Related

- [Send coins and tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/send-availability.md): Choose the right wallet, network, recipient and amount, then review and authorize a transfer.
- [Understand pending, confirmed and failed activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/transaction-status.md): Use status to distinguish a submitted transaction from a settled one.
- [Read the network fee](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/network-fee.md): See a transaction’s available fee converted to your chosen currency.

# Connect a dApp with WalletConnect

Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request.

WalletConnect support depends on the namespace and request method. Oath supports EVM, THORChain and Solana request flows within their implemented limits; it does not imply every network in the portfolio supports every dApp.

A familiar name or icon can be copied. Compare the website origin and reject unexpected, blocked or unverified requests when you cannot establish why they appeared.

Pairing requests expire. If the proposal is no longer usable, start a fresh connection from the dApp instead of reusing an old QR.

## Steps

1. Open the dApp from a trusted address and choose WalletConnect in its wallet connection options.
2. On another screen, scan its WalletConnect QR using Oath’s Home scanner. On the same device, choose the Oath link offered by the dApp.
3. Unlock Oath if asked. Read the connection proposal’s website identity and any verification warning.
4. Choose the intended wallet and approve only the networks you need. Review the methods being requested.
5. Connect, then return to the dApp. A connection shares the approved public accounts; it does not approve every future signature or transfer.
6. Review each later request independently. Manage the connection in Settings → WalletConnect or Permissions → Connected DApps.

Never share a WalletConnect pairing QR or URI publicly. Connecting does not require giving a site your recovery phrase or private key.

## Related

- [Disconnect a dApp safely](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-disconnect.md): End a WalletConnect session and separately review any on-chain permissions you granted.
- [Review a token swap from a dApp](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-swap.md): Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing.
- [Review wallet permissions and connected apps](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permissions.md): Inspect token allowances, NFT access, connected apps and supported account-control permissions for the selected wallet.

# Disconnect a dApp safely

End a WalletConnect session and separately review any on-chain permissions you granted.

A WalletConnect session allows a dApp to request actions. Disconnecting removes that session’s access to this wallet connection.

Disconnecting does not revoke on-chain allowances. A previously signed permit may also remain usable until its expiry or an applicable invalidation.

Disconnecting is not an on-chain transaction and does not reverse a completed swap or transfer.

## Steps

1. Open the connected-apps list and choose the wallet whose sessions you want to inspect.
2. Identify the session by its website and approved accounts/networks.
3. Open its controls and disconnect the intended session.
4. Return to the list and verify that it is no longer connected. Reconnect from the dApp if you later need it.
5. Open Permissions → Token access or Collectible access if you also want to revoke previously granted allowances.
6. Review and confirm those revocations separately, then check their results.

If a site still displays an old connected state, refresh it. Check Oath’s session list and on-chain permission status separately.

## Related

- [Connect a dApp with WalletConnect](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/connect-dapp.md): Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request.
- [Revoke a token allowance or delegate](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/revoke-token-access.md): Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.
- [Understand Permit2 and signed approvals](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permit2-access.md): Separate an existing allowance from a signature that may authorize future spending.
