# Review a token swap from a dApp

Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing.

For recognized router methods Oath displays readable swap bounds and routing operations. Native wrapping/unwrapping is only summarized when the route supports that interpretation.

A quote or simulation is not a guaranteed settlement price. Slippage, price movement, expiry and contract conditions can cause a swap to fail.

Unknown routers, commands or metadata remain explicitly unknown or technical. A safe review must not invent an output token or interpret every arbitrary contract call as a swap.

In 4.1.14, history recognizes supported Across and Relay bridge receipts and pairs matching outgoing and received legs. Unproven or unsupported transfers keep their ordinary history presentation. This does not add an in-app bridge service.

## Steps

1. Choose the input asset, output asset, amount and network in the dApp. Request its quote.
2. When Oath opens, confirm the dApp origin, selected wallet/account and network.
3. Read the input and output assets using their full identities. Check whether an amount is exact, a maximum input or a minimum output.
4. Review the recipient, native-coin value, network fee and deadline when shown. A token approval or Permit2 signature may arrive as a separate request before the swap.
5. Open Transaction data for readable operations and the original technical data. If an unfamiliar call cannot be explained, reject it until you can verify its purpose.
6. Confirm and authenticate only the request you intended. Return to the dApp for any remaining step, then verify the actual transaction outcome.

An approval grants spending access; it is not the swap itself. Verify the spender and limit, then review the separate swap request.

## Related

- [Read human-readable transaction data](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-transaction-data.md): Use the decoded details to understand a contract request while keeping the exact technical payload available.
- [Review messages, sign-ins and token permits](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-signatures.md): Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization.
- [Resolve a transfer that cannot be sent](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/send-troubleshooting.md): Work out whether the problem is validation, fees, authorization, provider access or an uncertain submission.

# Read human-readable transaction data

Use the decoded details to understand a contract request while keeping the exact technical payload available.

Decoding describes the submitted instructions; it does not certify a contract as safe or show every possible effect of its execution.

Token decimals are resolved for the exact asset. When reliable metadata is missing, exact raw units or addresses are safer than an invented name or amount.

Some complex or unsupported contracts cannot be completely decoded. Reject or independently verify those requests rather than assuming a generic label means a harmless transfer.

## Steps

1. On a transaction approval, check the network, account, destination contract and native value first.
2. Open Transaction data.
3. Read the recognized method and its fields: for example recipient, asset, spending limit, swap path or deadline.
4. For a batch or router execution, inspect each decoded operation, including any optional or unknown operation.
5. Use the technical/raw-data section when you need the exact selector or calldata. Do not approve simply because a method name looks familiar.
6. Return to the review and confirm only after the decoded operation agrees with your intended action.

Simulation is an estimate and can be incomplete. Always compare the exact network and contract with the dApp action you initiated.

## Related

- [Review a token swap from a dApp](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-swap.md): Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing.
- [Review messages, sign-ins and token permits](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-signatures.md): Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization.

# Review messages, sign-ins and token permits

Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization.

A message signature may have no immediate network fee but can still authorize an action. Permit signatures can grant spending rights when submitted later.

Signing a transaction and broadcasting it are distinct. A dApp can ask for signed bytes and submit them itself; the absence of an immediate History entry does not mean the signature is harmless.

A signature cannot generally be recalled by disconnecting the session. Available nonce invalidation and revocation mechanisms depend on the exact permission.

## Steps

1. Check which website requested the signature and why you expect it now.
2. Read the full message or structured fields. For sign-in, compare the domain, address and any expiry or nonce details.
3. For an approval or permit, inspect the token, spender, amount/limit, chain and deadline rather than treating it as a login.
4. If an editable approval limit is offered, choose only the allowance you intend and review the resulting request.
5. Reject unreadable, unexpected or unsupported requests. Authenticate only when the requested authorization makes sense.
6. After signing, return to the dApp. Manage any resulting on-chain allowance in Permissions.

No legitimate WalletConnect approval asks you to type a recovery phrase or private key into the requesting website.

## Related

- [Connect a dApp with WalletConnect](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/connect-dapp.md): Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request.
- [Understand Permit2 and signed approvals](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permit2-access.md): Separate an existing allowance from a signature that may authorize future spending.
- [Disconnect a dApp safely](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-disconnect.md): End a WalletConnect session and separately review any on-chain permissions you granted.

# Use Solana dApps and test networks

Review Solana requests on the exact mainnet, Devnet or Testnet cluster approved for the session.

The selected Solana derivation must match the account requested by the dApp. Switching accounts can invalidate a pending review.

Supported flows include readable message signing, legacy and version-0 transaction signing, supported transaction batches and sign-and-send. Unknown cluster aliases, unsupported versions and durable-nonce transactions are not silently converted to mainnet.

A batch is not a guarantee of atomic execution. Transactions that depend on an earlier batch member can fail independent simulation; Oath does not blindly approve them.

## Steps

1. In the dApp, choose the Solana cluster you intend to use and connect with WalletConnect.
2. Approve the requested cluster in Oath and verify the selected wallet/account. Devnet and Testnet are separate networks from mainnet.
3. When a request arrives, read its network, fee payer, fee and simulated SOL or token balance changes.
4. Inspect mint identities and invoked programs, particularly when a token name is unavailable or inspection is incomplete.
5. For a signing-only request, understand that the dApp receives a signed transaction. For sign-and-send, follow the pending result until confirmation or failure.
6. When testing, use only test-cluster assets and check the corresponding explorer. Test-cluster submissions do not become mainnet balances or mainnet history.

Third-party dApp compatibility varies. A test-cluster connection is not proof that every swap program or request is supported.

## Related

- [Connect a dApp with WalletConnect](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/connect-dapp.md): Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request.
- [Choose Phantom or Trust Wallet’s Solana path](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/solana-address-path.md): Match the Solana account derived by the wallet you are recovering.
- [Review a token swap from a dApp](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-swap.md): Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing.

# Review THORChain dApp requests

Check RUNE transfers, deposits and readable cross-chain swap instructions separately.

THORChain transactions can use memos to describe actions. A memo is operational data, not just a label for your records.

A cross-chain destination must be valid on that destination network. Do not substitute a same-looking address from another chain.

Unknown or unsupported instructions may not provide a complete readable preview. Verify them independently or reject them.

## Steps

1. Connect the intended THORChain account through the dApp’s WalletConnect flow.
2. Review the website and approved network before connecting.
3. For a transaction request, inspect the input asset, amount, destination and memo/deposit instructions.
4. For a recognized cross-chain swap, compare the receive asset and destination chain as well as the input chain.
5. Review the fee and any output bounds or deadline shown, then authenticate if you want to proceed.
6. Follow the transaction result and the dApp’s swap progress. A source-chain confirmation alone does not establish delivery on a different destination chain.

A direct RUNE send is different from a deposit or cross-chain swap. Review the action name and both sides of a swap.

# Revoke a token allowance or delegate

Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.

Removal uses the permission type’s supported instruction: for example an EVM/TRON allowance reset or a Solana token-account delegate revocation.

A transaction can confirm yet fail to remove the expected access if state changed or the contract behaves differently. Oath checks the resulting permission rather than relying only on a transaction hash.

An NFT collection approval, token allowance, account-control delegation and permanent token delegate have different scopes. Not every row can be revoked by the current account.

## Steps

1. Select the intended wallet in Permissions and wait for the scan.
2. Open Token access and locate the exact asset under its network heading. Compare the approved spender or delegate.
3. Swipe a removable row or open its detail and choose the removal action.
4. Review the wallet, network, approved address, access being removed and fee. Keep the relevant network fee coin available.
5. Confirm and authenticate when requested. Follow the pending result without resubmitting the same removal unnecessarily.
6. Open Recent changes and refresh the permission scan. Treat access as removed only after its result is verified.

Revoking access does not recover funds already spent by a contract. It also does not remove unrelated permissions.

## Related

- [Revoke several permissions](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/bulk-revoke-access.md): Select a group of permissions, review the batch and check each result independently.
- [Understand permission scan coverage](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permission-coverage.md): Use scan status to distinguish checked, partial, unavailable and unindexed network results.
- [Review wallet permissions and connected apps](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permissions.md): Inspect token allowances, NFT access, connected apps and supported account-control permissions for the selected wallet.

Canonical: https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/bulk-revoke-access
Updated: 2026-10-28T00:00:00Z
Applies to app version: Oath 4.1.14

# Revoke several permissions

Select a group of permissions, review the batch and check each result independently.

Each network can require its own transaction and fee. A batch is not a single atomic transaction and may finish with mixed results.

The queue can continue while the app is usable, but iOS can suspend background execution. Reopen and unlock Oath to resume when required; do not assume it runs indefinitely after closing the app.

Refresh coverage after completion. A request to revoke all selected entries does not discover previously unknown approvals or cancel arbitrary off-chain signatures.

## Steps

1. Open the access list for the wallet you intend to protect.
2. Use the filter menu to enter Select mode. Tap rows, Select All or Deselect All; review the visible network groups and selection count.
3. Tap Revoke All in the native bottom toolbar. This refers to your selected removable items, not every possible permission on every chain.
4. Review the batch, including network fees and items that cannot currently be prepared. Confirm only the permissions you intend to remove.
5. Authenticate when requested. You may continue using the app while the queue processes supported items; one failed item does not prevent later items from being attempted.
6. Open Recent changes. Check confirmed, pending and failed results individually, then correct failures and retry only the outstanding items.

Keep enough fee assets on every selected network. Never describe a partly successful batch as fully revoked.

## Related

- [Revoke a token allowance or delegate](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/revoke-token-access.md): Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.
- [Check revocation progress and failures](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permission-removal-history.md): Confirm each permission removal rather than assuming a completed queue means every item succeeded.
- [Understand permission scan coverage](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permission-coverage.md): Use scan status to distinguish checked, partial, unavailable and unindexed network results.

# Understand permission scan coverage

Use scan status to distinguish checked, partial, unavailable and unindexed network results.

A checked scan covers the implemented discovery method, not every possible contract or historical off-chain signature in the world.

Partial results can still contain useful permissions. Missing rows are not proof that access is absent; provider limits, custom contracts and unindexed data can prevent discovery.

Solana delegates, TRON approvals and EVM standard approvals differ. Coverage is reported per network rather than treating all accounts as interchangeable.

## Steps

1. Select the wallet you want to inspect.
2. Open Scan coverage and find the relevant network and last-check time.
3. Read whether the scan is checked, partial, unavailable or not indexed. Retry a failed or incomplete scan after checking connectivity.
4. Return to the access categories to inspect permissions that were actually discovered.
5. If you know an exact token contract and approved address, use Check a contract on a supported network.
6. Compare public on-chain state when needed and contact support with public network/contract details if a result remains unclear.

An empty permission list must not be interpreted as a comprehensive security audit.

## Related

- [Review wallet permissions and connected apps](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permissions.md): Inspect token allowances, NFT access, connected apps and supported account-control permissions for the selected wallet.
- [Check a contract and approved address](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/check-contract-access.md): Look up a specific supported permission when you know the exact contract and spender.

# Check a contract and approved address

Look up a specific supported permission when you know the exact contract and spender.

The approved address is the spender or operator, not automatically your own wallet address. A contract alone is not enough to identify an allowance.

Selecting a collection-wide approval is different from checking access to one NFT. Permit2 checks also need their appropriate token identity.

This targeted lookup does not scan every possible spender. It answers the specific supported permission query you supplied.

In 4.1.14, transaction history distinguishes supported token approvals, approval removal and contract interactions. A label describes the observed call; check its transaction status separately.

## Steps

1. Open Check a contract.
2. Choose the network using the network row with its logo.
3. Choose the access type you intend to inspect. The fields depend on that type.
4. Paste the token or collection contract and approved address into their connected fields. Enter a token ID or additional identity if the form requests it.
5. Compare the full addresses with trusted information, then tap the top checkmark.
6. Read the returned access and review a removal if supported. If the check fails, confirm the network and field formats before retrying.

Do not paste a private key or recovery phrase into either address field.

## Related

- [Revoke a token allowance or delegate](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/revoke-token-access.md): Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.

# Understand Permit2 and signed approvals

Separate an existing allowance from a signature that may authorize future spending.

Permit2 can involve multiple layers of authorization. Removing one current allowance is not a universal cancellation of every signature or spender.

Nonce invalidation is a different on-chain action from allowance removal. It applies to the supported nonce scope shown in the review, not arbitrary signatures across all protocols.

Unknown off-chain permits cannot be exhaustively discovered by scanning a wallet. Be cautious about signatures as well as transactions.

## Steps

1. Find the permission for the intended wallet, token, network and spender.
2. Read the current allowance and any expiry/nonce details provided.
3. Choose allowance removal when you want to remove the current supported on-chain access.
4. If a separate nonce-invalidation action is offered for the permission, read its purpose and review it independently.
5. Confirm the chosen action and fee, then check its verified result.
6. Disconnect unused dApp sessions separately and review other approvals for the same token.

An unlimited allowance is a spending authorization, not your token balance.

## Related

- [Review messages, sign-ins and token permits](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/dapp-signatures.md): Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization.
- [Revoke a token allowance or delegate](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/revoke-token-access.md): Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.

# Check revocation progress and failures

Confirm each permission removal rather than assuming a completed queue means every item succeeded.

Submission, chain confirmation and verification that access is removed are distinct stages.

A batch can continue after one error and therefore produce successful and failed rows together. Review all selected entries, not just the last notification.

Closing the app may pause work; reopening and unlocking allows supported pending work to resume.

## Steps

1. Open Permissions for the wallet used in the revocation.
2. Open the history/progress entry for the removal or batch.
3. Read each item’s network, asset, submission status and access result.
4. For pending items, wait and refresh or reopen Oath after connectivity returns.
5. For failures, read the reason, fix fee or network problems and prepare a new review for that item only.
6. Rescan the access list and compare the exact permission after confirmation.

Do not retry an uncertain transaction blindly. Use its existing public transaction ID to establish the outcome first.

## Related

- [Revoke several permissions](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/bulk-revoke-access.md): Select a group of permissions, review the batch and check each result independently.
- [Understand pending, confirmed and failed activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/transaction-status.md): Use status to distinguish a submitted transaction from a settled one.

# Review account-control and permanent delegates

Recognize permissions that affect more than a single token allowance.

Supported account-control inspection includes network-specific cases such as EVM delegation and TRON permission keys. These do not share one universal removal operation.

A Token-2022 permanent delegate is part of the mint’s authority design; an individual holder cannot simply revoke that authority like an ordinary token-account delegate.

A familiar asset logo or a small current balance does not make broad account control harmless. Read the scope before acting.

## Steps

1. Choose the intended wallet and open Account control.
2. Read the network, delegate or permission key and the scope shown for the entry.
3. Distinguish an account-control delegation from a token spending allowance.
4. If removal is offered, review exactly what it changes and whether the current wallet can authorize it.
5. Confirm only after checking the fee and result you expect. Verify the updated state after confirmation.
6. If the permission is permanent, unsupported or cannot be safely changed by this account, do not assume a token-level revoke will remove it.

When the app cannot safely remove a permission, it should remain a limitation rather than be reported as removed.

## Related

- [Review wallet permissions and connected apps](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permissions.md): Inspect token allowances, NFT access, connected apps and supported account-control permissions for the selected wallet.
- [Understand permission scan coverage](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/permission-coverage.md): Use scan status to distinguish checked, partial, unavailable and unindexed network results.
- [Revoke a token allowance or delegate](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/revoke-token-access.md): Remove a supported permission and verify that access is actually gone on-chain.

# Remove the last active wallet

Understand the final-wallet reset and clear Recently Deleted only after protecting your recovery options.

The final wallet is not left as the only item in Recently Deleted. The flow clears retained wallets before resetting the installation to its no-wallet state.

This removes local access and app data. Blockchain funds and previously granted on-chain permissions are unaffected; deleting a wallet does not revoke access.

Existing cloud backup files are separate. Keep the correct password and any extra recovery passphrase needed to restore them.

## Steps

1. Confirm you can recover the final wallet and any wallets in Recently Deleted before starting.
2. Choose remove for the last active wallet. Complete the applicable security authentication when asked.
3. If Recently Deleted contains wallets, review the first prompt and agree to include those wallets in permanent removal only if you have their required recovery material.
4. Read the final reset confirmation. Both confirmations must be accepted before deletion starts; cancel here if you need to preserve any wallet.
5. Confirm the final removal and wait for the local reset to finish. Do not interpret the first confirmation alone as completed deletion.
6. Oath returns to Welcome. To use a wallet again, import its recovery material or restore an encrypted backup.

Do not delete the last local copy of recovery material unless you have an independent, usable backup.

## Related

- [Move a wallet to Recently Deleted](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/remove-wallet.md): Remove a wallet from the active list while keeping a short recovery window.
- [Reset Oath on this device](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/reset-app.md): Erase local app data and return to setup.
- [Restore from an iCloud backup](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/restore-icloud.md): Recover a wallet from an encrypted Oath backup file.

# Open existing wallets after an Oath update

Unlock normally and let Oath prepare compatible existing wallets without creating replacements.

The upgrade preserves compatible wallet material and names using the new wallet rules. Unsupported multisig or multi-key collections are stopped safely rather than silently reduced to a different wallet.

An existing passcode is preserved where compatible. Biometric authorization can require a fresh system prompt; it must not be assumed from an old toggle alone.

Cached blockchain information is disposable and fetched again. An initially loading value is different from loss of the underlying wallet.

## Steps

1. Install the Oath update over the existing app; do not uninstall an app that contains your only usable recovery copy.
2. Open Oath and enter your existing app passcode if requested. Let the loading/unlock flow finish.
3. If biometric authorization needs to be renewed, enable it when offered or explicitly continue with passcode protection.
4. On Home, check the selected wallet and open Wallets to review the names of your other wallets.
5. Compare receiving addresses on the intended networks before transferring. Balances and history may take time to refresh.
6. If the upgrade cannot safely import a wallet type, stop and follow the error guidance rather than resetting or creating a replacement wallet over it.

Never send your passcode or recovery material to support. Keep the original recovery route until you have verified the upgraded wallets.

## Related

- [Unlock Oath](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/unlock-wallet.md): Use your app passcode or enabled biometrics to open the app.
- [Restore your wallets on another iPhone](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/move-to-new-phone.md): Use recovery material or an encrypted iCloud backup before removing the old installation.
- [Restore from an iCloud backup](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/restore-icloud.md): Recover a wallet from an encrypted Oath backup file.

# Understand the balance-change capsule

Read the observed change under the portfolio total without mistaking deposits for investment profit.

The change is based on available wallet-value snapshots. Deposits, withdrawals, asset discovery and market-price changes can all affect it.

Green and red help indicate direction; the text and sign remain important. A value change is not a tax report or a calculation of realized trading profit.

The capsule is a compact display. The removed balance-history bottom sheet and its range controls are not part of this flow.

## Steps

1. Open Home for the wallet you want to inspect.
2. Read the total and the change capsule underneath it.
3. Note the time period shown and whether the change is positive, negative or unchanged.
4. Review History for deposits, withdrawals and other activity that may have changed the balance.
5. Refresh to update available balances and market prices. Compare asset quantities when the currency value changes unexpectedly.

A missing or incomplete baseline can limit the comparison. Do not infer a full period of trading performance from a newly imported wallet.

## Related

- [Understand balances and portfolio value](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/portfolio-values.md): Oath shows token quantities and a local-currency valuation.
- [Refresh balances and activity](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/refresh-balances.md): Request updated data without leaving your wallet.

Narrow the portfolio by network and available asset filters without changing ownership.

# Understand token logos and missing prices

Distinguish token identity, balance, artwork and market data when searching by contract or mint.

Logos and quotes come from separate metadata and market-data paths. A token can have a valid logo and on-chain balance without a usable market quote.

Contract-based price lookup uses the exact chain and token reference and can consult multiple providers. Sparse liquidity, unsupported markets, rate limits or outages can still prevent a reliable price.

A quote is an estimate, not a promise that you can sell the entire holding at that price. Never use a logo or a displayed dollar value as evidence of contract safety.

## Steps

1. Paste the exact contract or mint address into asset search.
2. Compare the network and full identity of every matching result before adding one.
3. Open the asset and inspect its token quantity, logo and any available price separately.
4. If a price is unavailable, pull to refresh and wait for the price details to finish loading. A missing quote is not a confirmed price of zero.
5. Use Asset Information to compare the token identity with a trusted source. Do not match by ticker alone.
6. If the same supported token still has inconsistent artwork or prices, report its public contract/mint and network to support.

No provider can supply a trustworthy price for every token. Unknown prices should remain unavailable rather than fabricated.

## Related

- [Find and add a token by address](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/add-custom-token.md): Look up a supported contract or mint address and review its details before adding it.
- [Read an asset’s price and chart](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/prices-chart.md): View the latest available market quote and its recent movement.
- [Understand verified and manually added tokens](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/unverified-tokens.md): Learn why automatic discovery can omit a token and what changes when you choose to track it.

# Turn haptic feedback on or off

Choose whether Oath provides tactile feedback for supported controls and outcomes.

Haptics supplement visible labels, progress and results. A vibration is not proof that a blockchain transaction has confirmed.

Feedback depends on the device and supported interaction. A simulator cannot demonstrate how a physical device feels.

Turning feedback off does not change transaction checks, signing or network fees.

## Steps

1. Open Settings from the Home toolbar.
2. Find Haptic Feedback and change its switch.
3. Return to a normal selection or confirmation control to use the preference.

Read the on-screen status even when you feel success feedback.

# Use THORChain and RUNE

Receive RUNE, send on THORChain and distinguish a direct transfer from a dApp swap.

The native RUNE balance belongs to THORChain. A token with the same ticker on another chain is a different asset.

A direct send does not automatically execute a cross-chain swap. The dApp request must specify its deposit and swap instructions.

Keep enough RUNE for applicable fees and review any memo carefully.

## Steps

1. Open THORChain or search for RUNE in Wallet search.
2. Check the native quantity and use Receive for the THORChain address.
3. For a direct transfer, tap Send and enter the recipient and any required memo.
4. Review the amount, network and fee before authorizing.
5. After submission, check History and the public explorer record.
6. For a dApp deposit or cross-chain swap, review that separate WalletConnect request and its destination chain.

A source-chain confirmation alone does not prove a cross-chain destination payment is complete.

## Related

- [Review THORChain dApp requests](https://help.oathwallet.org/articles/walletconnect-thorchain.md): Check RUNE transfers, deposits and readable cross-chain swap instructions separately.

# Use HyperEVM in Oath

Find the correct HyperEVM account, native fee asset and tokens without confusing other EVM deployments.

HyperEVM uses an EVM account address, but its balances and token contracts are separate from other EVM chains.

Provider coverage for token discovery, logos, prices and history can differ. A missing quote is not a zero token balance.

Connecting a dApp requires its own network approval; adding an asset to Home does not authorize a dApp.

## Steps

1. Select Wallet, open Search and find HyperEVM.
2. Open the intended native asset or token and inspect Asset Information.
3. Use Receive to copy the public address for this network. Confirm the sending service offers the same network.
4. For tokens, search the exact contract address and verify the network before adding.
5. Use Send for supported transfers, keeping the native fee asset available.
6. Review History and open the transaction’s network-specific explorer after submission.

A shared 0x address does not bridge funds. Choose the exact network on both sides of a transfer.

# The Missing Link Between Open Source and the Wallet on Your Phone

Oath Wallet · October 19, 2026 · 9 min read

https://articles.oathwallet.org/open-source-wallets-verifiable-builds

What connects public source code to the app you install? A practical guide to reproducible builds, signed releases, App Store approval, and Oath’s current evidence.

You find a wallet with a public GitHub repository. The code is there. The license is there. People can inspect it, discuss it, and build it themselves. That is a meaningful reason to pay attention.

Then you open the App Store and tap Download.

One question still needs an answer: **was the app you just installed actually built from the code you were shown?**

For a wallet, that question reaches all the way to your money. The software on your phone helps generate or import credentials, displays the transaction you are about to authorize, and signs it. Being able to inspect the source is valuable. Being able to connect that source to the distributed app adds another layer of assurance.

Here is what that extra layer means, what it can prove, and how Oath describes the relationship between its public source and its App Store release.

## What open source gives you

Open-source software makes its code available under a license that grants rights to use, study, modify, and redistribute it. The Open Source Initiative’s definition includes those freedoms; simply putting some code on a public page does not automatically meet the definition. [Read the Open Source Definition.](https://opensource.org/osd)

For a wallet, public source lets independent developers examine questions that a marketing page cannot settle. How are keys generated? What gets stored? What leaves the device? What must happen before a transaction is signed? Which third-party libraries are involved?

That scrutiny matters even if you never read a line of code yourself. Researchers and other developers can investigate on your behalf and publish findings that everyone can inspect.

But a repository describes a body of code. On its own, it does not establish which code produced a particular download. A developer could publish one version and distribute another. A build system could also introduce an unwanted change after a reviewer has examined the source. Those are the gaps that build verification aims to reduce. [The Reproducible Builds project explains this threat.](https://reproducible-builds.org/docs/which-problems-do-reproducible-builds-solve/)

## What a reproducible build adds

A build turns source code into the software your device runs. A reproducible build makes that transformation repeatable: with the specified source, environment, and instructions, another party can produce identical copies of the defined output files. The comparison is usually made using cryptographic hashes. [See the formal definition.](https://reproducible-builds.org/docs/definition/)

A meaningful verification result therefore connects three things: an exact source revision, a documented build process, and a precisely identified release artifact. The report should show what was compared and whether it matched.

There is an extra step when the claim concerns an app store. Matching an unsigned file hosted on GitHub establishes a result about that file. To establish a result about the app on your phone, the evidence must also connect the comparison to the artifact delivered through that store.

Consider two otherwise comparable wallets. Both publish their source. For one, the connection between source and download rests on the publisher’s assurance. For the other, an independent party can rebuild the stated release and verify the distributed artifact using a documented method. The second offers stronger evidence against an undisclosed difference introduced during building or distribution. That is the specific security advantage.

## The word “verified” needs an object

Several useful checks are often described with the same word. They answer different questions.

**A verified GitHub commit** means GitHub has verified a commit’s cryptographic signature. It says something about the origin and integrity of that commit. It does not compare an App Store download with the repository. [GitHub documents exactly what its badge means.](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/managing-commit-signature-verification/about-commit-signature-verification)

**A successful build or test run** establishes that the stated build or tests completed in that environment. It does not establish that a store serves the same output.

**A signed release** provides evidence about the signer and the integrity of the signed artifact. A developer’s signature does not, by itself, demonstrate that the artifact was produced from public source.

**A build attestation** records provenance: information such as the source commit, repository, and workflow associated with an artifact. This is valuable evidence, but it still needs verification against the artifact and a sensible trust policy. GitHub explicitly warns that attestations do not guarantee an artifact is secure. [Read GitHub’s explanation of artifact attestations.](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/artifact-attestations)

**An independently reproduced release** adds a rebuild-and-compare result. A claim about the store version must identify how that result reaches the store-delivered app.

Before accepting “verified build,” ask: verified by whom, against what, and for which version?

## Apple’s approval and the source-to-store question

Apple’s review and code-signing system provide real protections. Apple describes developer identity checks, mandatory code signing, and review intended to check that apps generally work as described. These establish a controlled distribution process. They do not constitute a published comparison with a wallet’s GitHub source. [Apple explains its app code-signing process.](https://support.apple.com/en-mide/guide/security/sec7c917bf14/web)

The artifact itself also needs careful treatment. Apple’s app-thinning documentation describes device-specific variants containing different combinations of assets and binaries. A universal archive and a device-specific download can therefore be different files for legitimate reasons. [See Apple’s documentation on app variants.](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/Xcode/reducing-your-app-s-size)

A credible iOS verification method must identify the exact version and build, the source revision, the toolchain and configuration, and the particular artifact or components compared. It must explain how platform packaging and signing are handled. If any parts are excluded from comparison, the report needs to say which parts and why.

A matching version number, an archive checksum, or a successful upload is useful release bookkeeping. None of those facts alone closes the source-to-store gap.

When a wallet says its App Store build is verified, you should be able to follow a method and inspect a result, rather than infer a result from Apple’s approval.

## Google Play needs a precise claim, too

Android has practical tools for reproducible verification, but the distribution route still matters. Google Play can generate and sign optimized APKs from an Android App Bundle for different device configurations. Verifying an APK from a project’s website does not automatically verify every Play-delivered variant. [Google explains how App Bundles are distributed.](https://developer.android.com/guide/app-bundle)

F-Droid documents a concrete approach: reproduce the upstream APK, copy its signing information using the supported method, and check that verification succeeds. Its documentation explains both the required equivalence and common causes of mismatches. That is the kind of inspectable process a reproducibility claim should point to. [Read F-Droid’s reproducible-build documentation.](https://f-droid.org/docs/Reproducible_Builds/)

## How to compare wallets fairly

There are useful examples worth recognizing. Muun’s Android repository includes instructions for reproducible builds and for checking an existing APK: obtain the installed APK, select the corresponding source commit, and run its verification script. That goes beyond a general statement that the source is public. This article reviews the published procedure; it does not report a fresh verification of Muun’s current release, and the Android procedure should not be treated as proof for iOS. [Muun’s Android build and verification instructions.](https://github.com/muun/apollo/blob/master/BUILD.md)

Blockstream’s Android README documents another useful check: verifying release authenticity through certificate fingerprints and signed checksums. Those instructions help authenticate the download. The check described there answers a different question from independently rebuilding it. This is a distinction between the methods, not a claim that those instructions describe all of Blockstream’s security work. [Blockstream’s release-authenticity instructions.](https://github.com/Blockstream/green_android/blob/master/README.md#verifying-release-authenticity)

For any wallet that offers only a repository link, the fair conclusion is limited: public source is available, but that link alone supplies no evidence of a store-binary match. It would be wrong to turn that absence into an accusation of malicious behavior. It would also be wrong to advertise a match without evidence.

Compare the platform, release, method, and result. A brand-wide label hides too much.

## Oath: open source, and a clear statement about the shipped app

Oath publishes its MIT-licensed 4.1.14 (98) source release with build instructions and a release verification record. The app source used for the uploaded archive is commit v4.1.14. Provider configuration and Apple signing are supplied locally and excluded from Git. [Explore Oath’s published source release.](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/releases/tag/v4.1.14)

**On October 30, 2026, build 86 was uploaded to App Store Connect and submitted for review.** The [release verification record](https://github.com/devdasx/oath-wallet/releases/tag/v4.1.14) records the source, archive and upload evidence. Apple showed Waiting for Review at submission; the public US App Store listing still showed 4.1.2 when checked. Submission is not approval or a new public-store binary comparison.

There is a distinction worth keeping explicit: a publisher’s confirmation is not the same evidence as an independent party reproducing a release and publishing its comparison. This article does not present a new binary comparison, a byte-for-byte reproducibility result, or an independent security audit. The repository’s documented exclusions and configuration requirements still apply.

That distinction is the point of this article. Public source gives people something concrete to inspect. A maintainer’s release statement makes the team’s claim explicit. An independently repeatable comparison provides a further level of evidence. Readers should be able to tell which of those they are looking at.

For Oath, as for every wallet, security language should help people understand the evidence. It should never make them guess what “verified” means.

## Five things to look for before trusting a build claim

- **An exact release.** The platform, version, build number, and distribution channel should be unambiguous.

- **An exact source revision.** A fixed commit is more useful than a moving default branch.

- **A repeatable recipe.** Toolchain versions, dependencies, configuration, and required build inputs should be documented.

- **A transparent comparison.** Look for artifact identifiers, the comparison method, the result, and any exclusions.

- **A named verifier and a date.** Distinguish a publisher’s own checks from independent reproduction, and check whether the result applies to the version you use.

The [Reproducible Builds guidance on build environments](https://reproducible-builds.org/docs/perimeter/) explains why the toolchain and its assumptions need to be documented.

You should never need to share a recovery phrase or private key to investigate a public build-verification claim.

## Better evidence, with honest limits

A reproducible build can faithfully reproduce vulnerable code. It cannot, by itself, establish that the design is sound, that a remote service is trustworthy, or that your phone is uncompromised. Source review, security testing, careful dependency management, and responsible release practices still matter. Reproducibility addresses a particular gap in that larger system. [Read more about its purpose and limits.](https://reproducible-builds.org/docs/which-problems-do-reproducible-builds-solve/)

Open source makes inspection possible. Reproducible builds make a specified source-to-artifact relationship testable. Verification of the distributed app brings that evidence closer to the software you actually use.

For self-custody, those distinctions deserve plain language. A wallet should make it easy to see what has been checked, what the result proves, and what remains unproven. Confidence is more useful when you can trace where it comes from.

*Published October 19, 2026. Oath release evidence updated October 30, 2026. Oath’s source-correspondence statement is supplied by its maintainers. The technical explanations cite public documentation; this article is not an independent wallet audit or a new reproduction of an App Store or Google Play release.*

# Oath 3.5.5: A Better Feel for Every Transfer

Oath Editorial · September 14, 2026

https://articles.oathwallet.org/oath-3-5-5-slide-to-send-transaction-activity

Meet Slide to Send, clearer transaction activity, better Max fee handling, and simpler transaction details. A complete guide with real app screenshots and a hands-on video.

Sending a transaction has a few moments that deserve your full attention: the address, the amount, the fee, and the final decision to let it go. Everything around those moments should be easy to follow.

Oath 3.5.5 brings a new Slide to Send control, a clearer way to follow transactions, and more reliable fee handling when you use Max. It also tidies up the details you read afterward—and keeps ordinary screens where you left them when you return to the app.

This guide covers the changes across the 3.5.5 release, including the latest build, 59. The screenshots and video use Oath’s actual interface in iOS Simulator with demonstration balances, prices, addresses, and transaction results. No funds were signed or sent. The video’s confirmation timing is simulated; it is not a claim about network speed.

## Slide to Send: the final decision stays under your thumb

The last action on Review Transfer is now a slider. Three animated arrows and a soft shimmer show the direction to move. The control follows the language of the interface: left to right in English, right to left in Arabic and other right-to-left languages.

There is a useful distinction between reaching the end and letting go. Oath sends only when you release after completing at least 90% of the slide. Keeping your finger down at the end does not send the transaction. You can still move back below the threshold and release to cancel the gesture.

As you slide, the existing blue capsule becomes more pronounced. Light, stepped haptic feedback helps you feel your progress, with a softer approach to the end. The return motion follows the distance you have moved, so a short attempt and an almost-complete slide do not snap back in the same way. On supported devices, these small details make the control feel like something you move, rather than a button you happen to drag.

![Review Transfer in Oath 3.5.5 with a blue Slide to Send control.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/14115bc76ecb-review-transfer.webp)



Review Transfer with sample Dogecoin amounts and a demonstration recipient. The screen is a real Simulator capture; values are illustrative.

### How to use it

- Choose the asset and recipient, then enter the amount you want to send.

- On Review Transfer, check the network, recipient, amount, and fee. If you changed transaction options, review those too.

- Place your finger on the circular handle and slide in the direction of the arrows.

- Change your mind? Move back below 90% before lifting your finger, or release an incomplete slide. Nothing is submitted by that gesture.

- Ready? Complete the slide and lift your finger. A short animated checkmark appears in the handle before the review sheet closes.

That first checkmark acknowledges your completed gesture. It is not blockchain confirmation. The transaction still has to be submitted and accepted by the network; its progress appears in the activity capsule.[Watch the video](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/054e319a27e8-slide-to-send.mp4)

Video: the real Oath slider, recorded in Simulator with demonstration data. An incomplete slide returns; a completed slide waits for release. Submission and confirmation are simulated. No real funds were sent.

### When the fee is still loading

Before the transfer is ready, the slider explains what is happening with “Getting network fee…” and a native loading indicator in its handle. Once the fee is available and the transfer passes its checks, the control changes smoothly into its enabled state.

Returning to an unchanged transfer no longer unnecessarily starts the whole loading experience again. A usable fee presentation stays available while the app refreshes what it needs. Editing the transaction can still require new calculations, and network conditions can change. Always check the reviewed amount and fee before sending.

## One place to follow a transaction

After submission begins, a capsule appears near the top of Home. The asset’s logo stays visible, with a small badge that changes as the transaction progresses. You no longer have to interpret the same “sent to network” message at every stage.

- Sending… means Oath is working on submission. The badge is a loading indicator.

- Transaction Sent means the submission was accepted. A dot marks this stage; it is not a confirmation checkmark.

- Confirming… means the transaction is still waiting for the network’s confirmation. The badge shows a loading indicator.

- Transaction Confirmed means the app has received confirmation evidence. The badge becomes a green checkmark.

- Transaction Failed shows a danger badge. Open the transaction to read the specific result and any next step.

A connection problem or a temporarily unavailable result is not proof that a transaction failed. If the outcome is uncertain, Oath keeps that distinction rather than presenting an unverified success or failure.

### A capsule that gets out of the way

Once you have seen a Confirming or Confirmed capsule, it dismisses itself after three seconds. That countdown continues if you move to another screen; you do not have to return to Home and watch it again. You can also swipe it upward to hide it yourself. Sent and Failed states remain available until dismissed rather than disappearing on the same automatic timer.

If a transaction confirms while its capsule is still visible, the existing capsule changes to Confirmed. If the capsule has already gone away, the confirmation can appear again as a new update for that same transaction, then dismiss after three seconds. A later failure can also bring the capsule back so the result is not missed.

Swiping away the capsule only hides the notification. It does not cancel a transaction that has already been submitted.

### Several transfers? Open the bell

The bell beside the wallet selector appears when there is relevant transaction activity. Its number tells you how many items need attention. Tap it to open Activity, where you can follow pending incoming and outgoing transactions and relevant failures, then open an individual transaction for details.

The list keeps the information compact: the asset logo and status badge, the current status, the amount with its ticker, and a disclosure arrow. Repeated coin and network names have been removed from these rows. It uses the native navigation bar and close control, with the same glass presentation as the activity surface.

![Oath Activity showing a confirming transaction, amount, status badge, and disclosure arrow.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/a16131e41737-activity.webp)



Activity opens from the bell and keeps each transfer compact. This is a simulated pending transaction in the real app interface.

The small capsule continues to show one transaction at a time. The bell is the place to check the wider picture, especially if you send more than one transfer before the earlier ones confirm.

## Max now makes proper room for the fee

When you send a network’s native coin, the amount you can transfer must leave enough to pay that network’s costs. Choosing Max should account for that before you reach the final slide.

Version 3.5.5 improves this calculation, including a TRON issue where a Max transfer could fail with an insufficient-balance message even though the wallet had TRX. The available balance was being committed to the transfer before all applicable costs were properly reserved. Oath now makes room for the required costs before building the native TRX transfer.

For TRON, those costs can include bandwidth and, when applicable, recipient-account activation. Your resources, the recipient, and current network rules affect the result. A custom fee must also cover the required cost; setting it too low cannot make the network accept an underfunded transfer.

![TRON Review Transfer showing a demonstration amount and network fee.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/ebdbf3e134c1-tron-review.webp)



Illustrative TRON review: 98.9 TRX for the recipient and a 1.1 TRX fee from a 100 TRX demo balance. Actual fees vary.

Here is an illustrative example: if a wallet has 100 TRX and the required fee is 1.1 TRX, the transferable amount is 98.9 TRX. Those are demonstration numbers, not a fixed TRON fee. On networks that require an account reserve or a minimum remaining balance, that requirement must be retained too. Max means the maximum spendable amount, which is not always the entire displayed balance.

### Native coins and tokens work differently

For a native-coin transfer, Max accounts for the fee in that same coin. For a token transfer, you can send the token balance, but the network fee still needs to be funded separately with the native coin on that network.

For example, sending a TRC-20 token requires enough TRX for its network fee. Holding a large token balance does not by itself cover that fee. Oath checks the native fee balance; it does not automatically sell tokens or subtract a token quantity as a substitute for native gas.

To use Max, choose the correct asset and network, enter the recipient, tap Max on the amount screen, and review the resulting amount and Network Fee before completing the slide. If a fee or reserve leaves no spendable amount, add the required funds or choose a smaller transfer when appropriate.

## Bitcoin-family change: no more avoidable dust output

Bitcoin, Bitcoin Cash, Litecoin, and Dogecoin use unspent transaction outputs, or UTXOs. A transfer spends one or more outputs and usually returns the remainder to your wallet as change. That change is separate from the amount sent to the recipient.

Sometimes the leftover change is too small to create a valid, relayable output. This is called dust. A wallet can have enough total funds and still build a transaction the network rejects if it tries to create that tiny change output.

In 3.5.5, change below the applicable dust threshold is added to the network fee instead of being emitted as a dust UTXO. The calculation is handled consistently through review and transaction construction for the supported Bitcoin-family send paths.

This is particularly useful when spending several small outputs or sending almost everything. It removes an avoidable rejection without leaving a tiny output behind. The dust threshold depends on the network and output type, so there is no single dollar amount that applies everywhere.

The rule applies to the leftover change—not to the recipient’s payment. A recipient output that is itself below the network’s minimum still needs to be corrected. Always review the fee, including any small remainder absorbed into it. Coin Control remains available if you want to choose which UTXOs the transaction spends.

For more context on address types, derivation indexes, and Coin Control, see our [complete Bitcoin settings guide](https://articles.oathwallet.org/bitcoin-settings-oath-address-types-indexes-complete-guide).

## Confirmation and balance updates that follow the transfer

A transaction can be confirmed on-chain while a wallet is still showing older information. This release improves the checks behind pending transactions across the app’s supported networks, including the Bitcoin Cash path that could leave a completed transfer looking pending.

After a send, Oath begins refreshing the affected network’s balance after approximately two seconds and follows up as the transaction’s result becomes available. Failed or rejected attempts also prompt a balance refresh. Pending transaction tracking can resume when you reopen the app.

That two-second point is the start of a balance check, not a promise that a blockchain or its data provider will have updated within two seconds. A balance that has not changed does not prove a send failed: the provider may be behind, and a transfer between your own addresses may produce a different balance change from a payment to someone else. Transaction status and balance evidence need to be considered together.

The practical improvement is less waiting for Oath to catch up after new information becomes available. It does not make blocks arrive faster, change a network’s finality rules, or allow unlimited polling while iOS has suspended the app.

## Transaction details, with less repetition

The transaction screen has been simplified around the information you actually need to inspect. “Confirmation Pending” is now the shorter “Pending.” “Blockchain Network” becomes “Network,” and “Transfer Amount” becomes “Amount.” The network appears once in the overview rather than being repeated in the transfer summary.

The Transfer Summary now brings Amount and Network Fee together. The separate Value and Fee in US Dollar rows are gone. Both summary values start in your selected local currency; tap an available value to switch it to the relevant cryptocurrency unit, then tap again to switch back.

![Oath transaction details with confirmed status and local-currency Amount and Network Fee.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/273186040128-transaction-details.webp)



The simplified Transfer Summary brings Amount and Network Fee together. All transaction data shown here is demonstration data.

This keeps the summary short without taking away the precise coin amount. For a token transfer, remember that the amount and fee may be denominated in different assets: the token you sent and the native coin that paid the fee.

![The same transaction details after tapping Amount to display 25 DOGE.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/153a529d4472-transaction-details-units.webp)



Tap Amount to switch the same value from local currency to cryptocurrency units. The fee has its own display toggle.

Interactive values now use the same neutral text treatment as the other fields. A disclosure arrow is reserved for a row that opens another screen or sheet. Tapping an amount to change its display does not need a navigation arrow because you stay on the same screen.

The transaction hash, sender, recipient, status, and local notes are still there when you need them. Notes remain on your iPhone and are not written into the blockchain transaction.

## Come back to the screen you left

If you leave Oath while an ordinary transaction sheet is open, returning after a few minutes should not unexpectedly close it. Version 3.5.5 preserves that presentation while the app remains in memory, so you can continue reading where you stopped.

Screens that reveal sensitive wallet material are treated differently. A recovery phrase, private key, or other secret-reveal screen closes after about 20 seconds away. Your existing App Lock settings continue to apply; this change does not remove them.

As with other iOS apps, force-quitting the app or having iOS terminate it is different from switching away and returning. This improvement concerns resuming the running app, not a promise to restore every open sheet after a fresh launch.

## A quieter Home and a tidier Receive screen

Home opens without the previous fade-and-scale entrance. The bottom settings control now uses a gear icon, making its purpose easier to recognize next to search.

Receive’s network filters have also been refined. The spacing beneath the title is tighter, and the chips fit their text and circular network artwork more naturally. Tap a network to narrow the asset list, or choose All to see the broader selection.

![Oath Receive asset selector with network filter chips beneath the title.](https://oathwallet.org/assets/articles/5e341905567f-receive.webp)



Receive uses content-sized network chips and tighter spacing beneath the navigation title. Assets and balances are samples.

Temporary refresh problems also receive better handling. Existing wallet content can remain visible instead of being interrupted by the technical wallet-refresh alert that exposed a timeout code. A temporary inability to refresh is not the same as losing your wallet or your funds.

Account-activation guidance is more selective too. On networks with a genuine activation or funding requirement, the amount screen surfaces the relevant shortfall when it matters. It avoids showing an unnecessary “not active” warning when the entered amount already satisfies the applicable requirement.

## A few more fixes worth knowing about

- Backup and private-key messages are clearer, with more specific wording for the material or action involved.

- Import handles rejected phrase entries more cleanly when you choose to try a different phrase.

- The send activity flow includes fixes for a background queue crash and for capsules that could linger after you had already seen them.

- Slider movement, direction, and feedback have been refined for both left-to-right and right-to-left interfaces, including a smoother return while you move your finger back.

The common thread is straightforward: give you a clearer decision before a transfer, a clearer result afterward, and fewer interruptions in between.

## Getting 3.5.5

Oath 3.5.5 is available on the [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/app/id6780187283). Open the listing on your iPhone or iPad and choose Update if you already have Oath installed.

Once installed, the in-app Version History contains the notes for your exact version and build. Start with a transfer you can review carefully: check the recipient, inspect the fee, try moving the slider and returning it, and only complete and release it when you are ready to submit.
